title: Breakouts & wildcards - 13 surprise stars for new season
description: BBC Sport TV and radio commentators identify the players they think could be the breakout stars of the new Premier League season.
fullText:
Eli Junior Kroupi, Igor Thiago and Nico O'Reilly were among the breakout stars who made their mark on the Premier League last season - but who will be next?

BBC Sport's TV and radio commentators have picked 13 players they believe are worth watching out for over the next few months.

Whether they are new signings, wonder kids or late bloomers, here are some unfamiliar faces of all ages who might make a name for themselves in the new campaign.

Age: 18 Position: Centre-midfield Country: Netherlands

Steve Bower: There has been a lot of talk this summer about Newcastle players departing, particularly in the midfield area, but here's someone they brought in early on - before Eddie Howe left - in a deal that could be worth up to £23m.

I saw Steur play in Europe for Ajax last season, and he made 25 appearances for them in all competitions in the end. He can either play in defensive midfield or a bit further forward, is two-footed and has lovely passing ability.

Obviously it is a big step up, as we know, to come from the Dutch league into the Premier League as a teenager, and also to arrive at a club in transition with a new manager.

But Newcastle have got players like Lewis Miley - who has come through in recent seasons - that Steur can learn from being in a similar situation as well.

I liked the look of him on first viewing for Ajax and he appears as if he has got the personality to play in the Premier League.

Steur is not someone who necessarily starts initially, or all the time, but he seems pretty fearless and is the type of player who could grab the opportunity if it comes his way.

Age: 20 Position: Midfield Country: Ghana

John Murray: This looks a potentially shrewd signing for newly promoted Coventry City, even though they have just paid a club record transfer fee of about £25m to sign him from Danish side FC Nordsjaelland.

Yirenkyi featured in all four of Ghana's matches at the World Cup and, when I commentated on him during their group match against England, I thought he looked the kind of energetic midfielder who would do well in the Premier League.

Conor McNamara: Coventry City have got themselves a talented and versatile new signing in Yirenkyi - which is pronounced 'yur'INCH-ee', by the way.

He started on the right of a back five for Ghana against England at the World Cup, but his favoured position is the centre of midfield.

Wales fans will remember him scoring against them in the pre-tournament friendly in June and he got a goal at the World Cup itself against Panama too.

After coming through Ghana's 'Right To Dream Academy', he was named Young Player Of The Year in the Danish Superliga last season with Nordsjaelland.

Frank Lampard could be just the right coach to help Yirenkyi blossom further, as a midfielder of Premier League standard.

Age: 27 Position: Defender Country: Spain

Conor McNamara: Mingueza did not make Spain's World Cup-winning squad, but the standard was incredibly high. Pedro Porro was first choice right-back and, with Marcos Llorente and Marc Pubill also able to cover that position, Mingueza was left to rue what might have been.

After allowing his contract to run down at Celta Vigo, the defender has joined Crystal Palace on a free transfer, which might just prove to be one of the signings of the summer. I commentated on Mingueza playing for Spain at the Nations League finals a year ago and he is very impressive at turning defence into attack.

With Daniel Munoz's future at Selhurst Park up in the air, Mingueza could be a ready-made replacement for one of Palace's most effective players of recent seasons.

If Munoz stays, Mingueza has the versatility to play anywhere across the back line.

Age: 17 Position: Striker Country: England

John Murray: Madjo is a teenage striker Aston Villa fans will know all about already after the goals he has scored for them in pre-season.

Born in London to parents from Cameroon, Madjo grew up in Luxembourg and made his senior international debut for them last year.

But he has now switched his international allegiance to England and played for the Under-17 team.

After a wrangle over that, he was finally cleared to play in competitive matches for Villa, making his competitive debut last week with a goal in the Super Cup against Paris St-Germain.

He looks like a big man with a big future.

Guy Mowbray: There's been talk of a loan move for Madjo, but his flurry of pre-season goals and a massive impact against PSG should keep him around at least until the next transfer window.

If that's the case - you won't fail to notice him! He is a powerful striker who has most of the tools to be a success.

Steve Bower: I was going to choose Johan Manzambi, who I included when we did a similar article about new players to watch at the World Cup. Manzambi had an excellent tournament, and Villa pipped Newcastle to sign him.

But I didn't want to include two players from one club, and I was told about Madjo when Villa signed him for just over £10m back in January, before they had well-documented issues registering him.

Obviously we know he has been available in pre-season, when he has made his mark with four goals against Walsall, Real Sociedad and Indonesia All-Stars. Then of course Unai Emery gave him his opportunity against PSG, when he scored again.

He has got a huge frame and figure for his age, bringing very early comparisons to Erling Haaland, which is a big tag to carry.

But, without putting too much pressure on a 17-year-old's shoulders, with Villa being in the Champions League this season and the extra games that brings, Madjo is going to get some minutes.

It feels like the perfect scenario for Madjo, because with strikers like Ollie Watkins and Tammy Abraham at the club, Villa can introduce a young player like him to the first team without having to rely on him.

In Emery, Madjo has got the perfect manager to nurture his development too, and I think he could make his mark across all competitions this season.

Age: 18 Position: Centre-back Country: Australia

Conor McNamara: I saw Herrington start for Australia at the World Cup and was impressed by his calm assurance on the ball.

He only turns 19 at the start of September and is very young for any central defender in the Premier League, so it is going to be a steep learning curve for him, but he is robust at 6ft 4in, which will help.

Herrington has played just one season in Major League Soccer with the Colorado Rapids, but he did well enough to be named in the MLS All-Stars Team. He only made his international debut in March, but became Australia's youngest starter in a World Cup game as they reached the knockout stages.

It was Herrington's penalty - blasted against the crossbar - that ultimately eliminated Australia from the tournament in their last-32 shootout defeat by Egypt.

But the fact he was given the responsibility of that crucial kick, and that he was willing to take on the challenge, shows he has immense courage.

Age: 19 Position: Centre-back Country: Serbia

Tom Gayle: Bournemouth are renowned for their 'plug and play' approach to recruitment.

Dean Huijsen, Milos Kerkez and Illia Zabarnyi arrived with low profiles and were all trusted with regular Premier League minutes before all three moved on in return for significant transfer fees.

Veljko Milosavljevic could be their latest defensive recruit to attempt to follow a similar trajectory.

I was at Vitality Stadium 11 months ago that the teenager made his debut in Bournemouth's 2-1 victory over Brighton. Before the match there was surprising honesty from then head coach Andoni Iraola, who told me he was unsure if Milosavljevic was ready for the Premier League.

The context was that Iraola had only worked with the youngster for just a couple of days because the defender had been away with Serbia's Under-21 team.

But he was ready, and made a further six top-flight appearances before suffering a knee injury in December's defeat by Everton, which remains his last Premier League outing.

Granted, it's a limited sample size, but his cameos provided clear evidence Milosavljevic possesses the technical ability and physicality required to earn more consistent game time.

A knock picked up during pre-season may mean a delayed start to the campaign but, fitness permitting, I'm excited at the prospect of seeing more of a man described as "one of the biggest talents of Serbian football" by media in his homeland.

Age: 19 Position: Centre-midfield Country: England

Steve Wilson: The young central midfielder has been one of Liverpool's best performers in pre-season. Signed from Leicester City in 2023, he made his Premier League debut in late December after a handful of appearances in domestic cup competitions.

Arne Slot liked what he saw enough to give the then 18-year-old a dozen appearances from the bench in the second half of last season.

Andoni Iraola has been impressed by Nyoni on his new side's somewhat shaky US tour and, with central midfield an area Liverpool aren't especially strong in, he may be reconsidering listening to offers to send him out on loan.

Age: 20 Position: Left-winger Country: Ivory Coast

Steve Wilson: After a difficult summer, Newcastle will be hoping Toure can make an early impact, just as he did when he joined Hoffenheim from Hammarby only 18 months ago.

Fifteen assists and five goals during his time in the Bundesliga meant that comparisons with countryman Yan Diomande at RB Leipzig were inevitable. 'Bazoumania' burned brightly but only briefly in south-west Germany.

Toure - who is only eight months older than Diomande, now of Real Madrid - prefers to operate down the left flank, although he can be effective on both sides.

Combining his pace with control is not easy, but Toure has worked hard on providing an end product to go with his acceleration.

His one start and two substitute appearances at the World Cup for Ivory Coast were slightly underwhelming but with Diomande and Amad Diallo also in the squad, competition for places out wide was fierce.

Age: 19 Position: Midfield Country: England

Guy Mowbray: The exits of Youri Tielemans and Morgan Rogers have left a big gap to fill in Aston Villa's midfield.

Hemmings looks like a mixture of the two players who have departed and his display against PSG in the Super Cup caught my eye as much as, if not more than, Madjo's. He looks confident and classy on the ball.

Tom Gayle: There is hole in Villa's midfield as a result of Tielemans' move to Manchester United as well as Amadou Onana's anterior cruciate ligament injury. Unai Emery will hope Hemmings could be the solution.

A regular England international throughout the age groups, Hemmings had plenty of admirers as he progressed through the Nottingham Forest academy before moving to the West Midlands at the start of 2024.

Back in January, I was in the press box for his first senior start in the Europa League group match against Salzburg. With Villa trailing 1-0 at half-time, the teenager - who in my assessment had struggled - was taken off.

I concluded Hemmings must have been substituted because of his performance, but Emery confirmed afterwards the plan was always for him to play just 45 minutes.

There's no doubt during the 20 months since his arrival at Villa's Bodymoor Heath training ground that Hemmings has been nurtured in the strict requirements of 'Emery Ball'. The Spanish head coach has admitted during this time the youngster has spent more time "working and not playing".

All this work behind the scenes led to John McGinn's striking assessment of Hemmings' performance against PSG, when he proclaimed "it's no surprise to see him as one of the best players on the pitch".

Following his breakout performance last week, perhaps the only surprise will be if we don't get to see a lot more of Hemmings this season.

Age: 19 Position: Centre-back Country: Croatia

Steve Wilson: Playing for just over an hour at the World Cup for Croatia would have come as a disappointment to the teenager, who had just enjoyed a stellar season at Hamburg on loan from Tottenham.

Brighton knew what they were doing when they made signing Vuskovic a condition of selling Jan Paul van Hecke to Spurs. Not only was he one of the best young defenders in Germany last season, he was also the Bundesliga's top-scoring centre-back.

Vuskovic looks ready to come straight into top-flight action, and how many signings do Brighton get wrong?

Age: 18 Position: Winger Country: England

Guy Mowbray: What happens at Etihad Stadium this season is something of an unknown post-Pep Guardiola, but as Enzo Maresca assesses the riches he has available, he might just be impressed by the talent of the teenager recruited from Chelsea's academy.

The FA Youth Cup-winning winger looked at home with the senior players on City's Far East tour, with his chances of a regular place on the bench likely to be enhanced if, as expected, Savinho moves on.

Age: 19 Position: Forward Country: England

Steve Bower: At Manchester United, everyone is talking about JJ Gabriel, who is so good he is a freak of nature - but he is just 15, so we might only see him occasionally in the Carabao Cup this season.

A few years ahead of him, but still only 19, is Shea Lacey, who has overcome some early injury problems and has figured prominently in pre-season.

Lacey is an exciting wide player - exactly the type that United fans like - and is also very well known to Michael Carrick, not only with his coaching head on but also his parental one, from watching his son Jacey over the years in United's academy.

I watched Lacey play against Burnley in United's first game under Darren Fletcher, another coach who knows him well, when he took temporary charge last season.

A lifelong United fan, he was a whisker away from scoring in that game at Turf Moor and I see him being involved in the first-team squad a lot this season.

He is fearless, and it doesn't look like the shirt or any expectation will weigh heavily on him. United fans are going to enjoy seeing a lot more of him this season, with Carrick keen to give him as many opportunities as possible.

Age: 19 Position: Midfield/forward Country: Switzerland

James Fielden: I first saw Johan play for Freiburg towards the back end of last season in their Europa League tie against Celta Vigo and said to a colleague that something would have gone wrong for him if he wasn't playing Premier League football come August. Think of Eberechi Eze in the way he effortlessly glides across the pitch with the ball.

Don't be fooled by the number nine he wore on his back for Switzerland at the World Cup - he generally plays a lot deeper than that.

He played against Villa in their Istanbul final, but him not having much of a say was more about the team than his own doing.

Steve Wilson: He went into the World Cup with his reputation blossoming after helping Freiburg reach the Europa League final, and came out of the World Cup looking like the future of Swiss football, with Newcastle and Villa hot on his heels.

His brace against Bosnia and goal against Canada meant Freiburg had little choice but to cash in.

Manzambi can play in central midfield, as a number 10 or as a right-sided forward - which is arguably his most effective position. Switzerland missed him badly when injury curtailed his World Cup in the last 32.

title: £2.14bn and counting - why Premier League spending could set new record
description: Premier League clubs have spent £2.14bn this summer, with huge sums moving between top-flight rivals. BBC Sport examines the possibility of a new spending record.
fullText:
Premier League clubs have already spent £2.14bn during the summer transfer window, with more than two weeks still remaining before the deadline.

That total is already higher than the full summer outlay in 2024 (£1.98bn), 2022 (£1.94bn), 2021 (£1.13bn) and 2020 (£1.32bn), according to figures provided to BBC Sport by Paul Macdonald, founder of FootballTransfers.com.

Only 2023 (£2.36bn) and last summer's record £3.14bn currently sit above it.

Another record-breaking window therefore remains possible. But the more revealing story may be not simply how much Premier League clubs are spending, but where that money is going.

The financial gap between England and the rest of Europe is stark.

Premier League clubs have spent £2.14bn this summer, compared with £780m in Serie A, £515m in La Liga, £505m in the Bundesliga and £412m in Ligue 1.

That means England's top flight has already spent more than those four other major European leagues combined.

Chelsea are leading the way, having committed £348m so far this summer, comfortably ahead of every other Premier League club. Tottenham are next, on £228m, with Arsenal and Manchester City both on £151m. Chelsea, Tottenham and City have all broken their club transfer record during the window.

But the spending is not confined to the elite. Aston Villa, Brentford, Brighton and Leeds United have also made their most expensive signing ever this summer. Coventry City, Hull City and Ipswich Town, the three promoted clubs, complete the list, underlining how widely spending power now stretches across the division.

Taking the whole of 2026 into account, and including Crystal Palace's signing of Jorgen Strand Larsen in January, 11 of the 20 Premier League clubs have broken their transfer record during the calendar year.

One of the clearest features of this summer's window has been the amount of business taking place between Premier League clubs.

Almost £785m has already been spent on intra-league transfers - players moving between one English top-flight club and another - with eight of the 12 biggest Premier League signings so far this summer falling into this category.

It's a trend that extends beyond a single summer. Intra-Premier League spending reached £1.29bn last season, the highest summer figure since 2016. This summer's in-house outlay so far represents almost a third of all Premier League transfer expenditure.

The proportion is not unprecedented - 35.9% of spending stayed within the league last season and 37% did so in 2017-18 - but the cash sums involved are now substantially larger.

The so-called Big Six - Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham - have been central to that spending.

They have already paid £546.5m this summer to recruit players from non-Big Six Premier League clubs. Last season, that figure reached a record £647m, while the Big Six have paid almost £3bn has moved from the Big Six to other Premier League sides in transfer fees since summer 2016.

Chelsea have been the most active club in the Premier League's internal market since 2016-17, spending £867m and receiving £683m in deals with fellow top-flight sides.

Some of those moves have dramatically reshaped individual careers and rivalries. Morgan Rogers and Elliot Anderson, both England internationals and members of the Three Lions squad at the 2026 World Cup, have joined new clubs. Rogers has left Aston Villa for Chelsea, while Anderson has departed Nottingham Forest for Manchester City.

Former Newcastle midfield partners Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes have gone their separate ways too, joining opposite sides of the north London divide at Tottenham and Arsenal.

Of the seven £100m-plus transfers to a Big Six side from another Premier League club since 2016, three have taken place this summer: Rogers, Anderson and Tonali.

There is a sporting and financial logic to that kind of recruitment. Players who have already performed in the Premier League offer buying clubs evidence that they can handle the competition, reducing some of the uncertainty that can accompany moves from overseas.

For the selling club, a major domestic transfer can be equally significant. Large fees can create greater flexibility under squad-cost and profitability rules, allowing clubs to reinvest elsewhere in the squad.

Gross spending tells only part of the story. Premier League clubs have received £1.28bn in transfer fees this summer, leaving the division with a net spend of £856m.

That still dwarfs the other major leagues. Serie A's net spend stands at £320m and La Liga's at £185m, while the Bundesliga and Ligue 1 are currently net sellers.

Within England, Chelsea have the biggest negative balance at £209.5m, followed by Arsenal at £111.6m and Manchester City at £92m.

Chelsea's position is part of a longer-term pattern. Across the past five seasons, their cumulative net spend stands at about £977m, the highest among the clubs examined.

At the other end of the market, Newcastle have received £226m in fees this summer, Aston Villa £199.5m and Nottingham Forest £123m. Crystal Palace and Sunderland have also recorded a positive transfer balance.

Villa currently have the biggest positive net balance among those clubs at £109.8m, followed by Newcastle at £88.5m and Forest at £71.8m.

The figures highlight how differently clubs are operating in this summer's market, with some among the biggest net spenders while others have generated considerable income from player sales.

Last summer's £3.14bn remains some way ahead of the current £2.14bn total, so another record cannot yet be assumed.

But the window still has time to run, and Premier League clubs are already spending at a level unmatched anywhere else in Europe.

Whether £3.14bn is eventually surpassed or not, this summer has already demonstrated two things: transfer records are falling across the division, while many of the window's biggest deals are being conducted between Premier League clubs themselves.

title: Stats that show Premier League is getting more competitive
description: Last season, the Premier League was arguably more competitive than it has been for years. BBC Sport looks at whether that will continue to be the case this time around.
fullText:
Last season, the Premier League was arguably more competitive than it has been for years.

While the 65 points between champions Arsenal and bottom side Wolves was around the average for a 38-game season (63), a real revolution took place in mid-table.

Since the league was reduced to 20 teams in 1995-96, the gap between the top four and the bottom three – between what has often been the Champions League and the Championship – had been increasing as the seasons went by, with the 'bigger' clubs profiting from their European adventures and the extra money they earned by regularly finishing higher in the table.

But last season, the gap between the 'haves' and the 'have-nots' of the Premier League dropped from 44 points in 2024-25 to just 26 points – the smallest distance for 23 years (since 25 points in 2002-03).

The European places were more attainable than they had been for years. Despite taking a point fewer than when they finished seventh the season before, Aston Villa clinched Champions League qualification by finishing two places higher.

While Liverpool took the 'bonus' Champions League place by finishing fifth, their points total of 60 was the lowest by a side finishing there for 19 years and would have put them ninth in 2024-25.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also took full advantage of needing fewer points than normal by qualifying for European competition for the first time ever and for over half a century respectively.

Meanwhile, the teams in the bottom half finished with more points than they had in years, meaning that judging them simply by their position in the table is perhaps a little harsh.

Everton may have been underwhelmed with their 13th-place finish but it was the most points a team in that position had finished with since the Toffees themselves did it at the turn of the millennium.

The points of the four places below them were all the highest they have been in the Premier League for 23 years and West Ham can consider themselves unlucky to have gone down with the highest points total for an 18th-placed side since 2010-11.

Overall, 13 of the 20 teams finished with between 40 and 60 points last season – the most in a Premier League campaign since 2003-04 (also 13).

Was the Premier League so competitive in 2025-26 because the quality of the 'lesser' teams got better or the top teams got worse? It is hard to know for sure.

Given how savvy smaller clubs like Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, the vast amounts of money that enable even bottom-half sides to poach the best talent from abroad and the Premier League's current dominance of the Europa League and Conference League, it would seem to be the former.

However, the fact that promoted play-off winners Sunderland were able to finish above 13 teams in their first season back suggests the league was maybe not as strong as we think.

What we do know is that whether because they got worse or their opponents got better, four of the sides that finished in the top seven in 2024-25 – champions Liverpool, Chelsea, Newcastle and Nottingham Forest – took 79 points fewer between them last season.

While Forest's decline was perhaps expected given their incredible seventh-place finish in 2024-25 and their journey to the Europa League semi-finals last season, the others were far more surprising.

Sunderland and Leeds smashed the recent run of promoted sides struggling to compete by taking 64 more points than the teams they replaced in the top flight.

As a result, this season will be a bit of an upside-down one in that Bournemouth, Brighton and Sunderland have European campaigns to navigate while Chelsea, Tottenham and Newcastle do not.

Will we therefore see a bounce-back to the more 'traditional' order in 2026-27 or are we truly entering a new, fiercely-competitive era of the Premier League?

However, one place where the Premier League has become less competitive – likely because it has become more fiercely-contested overall – is at the very bottom.

While it is almost expected for one side to be cut adrift long before the end of the season, nowadays two sides are getting left behind.

The average points tally of the second-bottom side in a 38-game season is 31, meaning teams that finish there have usually competed in a relegation battle for most of the season before ultimately falling short.

After the Premier League was reduced to 20 teams in 1995-96, only two 19th-placed sides failed to reach 30 points in the first 21 seasons. But in the last decade, seven of the 10 sides to finish in that position have failed to do so.

In fact, in the past two seasons promoted sides Ipswich and Burnley have both finished there with just 22 points – the fewest ever taken by a second-bottom side.

Relegation battles are now mostly a fight to see who takes the final spot in the bottom three, with the other two accounted for long before the final day – often by promoted sides.

But inspired by the survival of Sunderland and Leeds, promoted Coventry City, Ipswich Town and Hull City will all be hoping they have what it takes to match the competitiveness of the Premier League this season.

title: These eight players will help you win FPL
description: Our Fantasy Premier League experts pick eight players they think will help you have a successful FPL season.
fullText:
Have you settled on your Fantasy Premier League team yet, or are you still at the tinkering stage?

Either way you may want to consider one of these players in your team, according to our FPL experts.

Here are the eight players - aside from the obvious premium picks such as Bruno Fernandes and Erling Haaland - we think can help you have a successful season.

You can join the BBC Sport League on the official Fantasy Premier League game using the code bbcfpl - or by clicking this link, external.

Florian Wirtz, Liverpool, midfielder, £7.5m

Wirtz at £7.5m with around 14% ownership looks like one of the better mid-priced differentials available right now. While nearly half the game has locked in Dominik Szoboszlai, far fewer managers are backing the German, which creates useful rank upside if he delivers.

Under new manager Andoni Iraola, the picture is getting clearer. Pre-season has seen Wirtz deployed as a proper number 10, operating close to striker Alexander Isak.

Iraola has spoken openly about wanting Wirtz in that central role behind the striker rather than pushed wide, and the early friendlies have reflected that. Playing higher up the pitch should mean more touches in the final third and a greater share of Liverpool's goal involvement.

Last season, Wirtz showed quality without fully maximising his output. A second year in the Premier League, combined with a manager who seems determined to get the best out of both him and Isak, improves the outlook. At this price and ownership level, he offers a cleaner route into Liverpool's attack than many of the more popular midfield options.

Pascal Gross, Brighton, midfielder, £5.5m

Gross is one of the more compelling budget midfielders available, and is currently owned by fewer than 11% of teams. He is not flashy, but his underlying role and importance has improved significantly this summer.

With Danny Welbeck now at Chelsea, Gross should take over penalty duties. He converted a spot-kick in pre-season against Strasbourg and also delivered a free-kick assist in the same match. Add his existing involvement in corners and other set-pieces and you have multiple routes to returns that most £5.5m midfielders simply do not possess.

Brighton under Fabian Hurzeler continue to generate chances, and Gross remains central to how they progress the ball and attack dead balls. He is trusted for minutes when fit and offers a reliable floor plus occasional ceiling at a price that helps fund the big hitters elsewhere.

For managers building around expensive premiums, Gross is a practical enabler who can quietly accumulate points without demanding a large slice of the budget.

Antonin Kinsky, Tottenham, goalkeeper, £4.5m

Kinsky looks like one of the standout budget goalkeeper options this season, particularly if he can hold on to the starting place at Tottenham. The Czech goalkeeper finished last season strongly, starting every game under Roberto de Zerbi and producing several excellent performances.

There is still some uncertainty, with Guglielmo Vicario still at the club. However, Kinsky is seemingly De Zerbi's first choice. He stuck with Kinsky for Tottenham's run-in last season, even after Vicario returned from injury, which showed how highly he was regarded.

At £4.5m, Kinsky doesn't need to produce huge returns to justify his place in your FPL team. If he can remain Spurs' first choice, the combination of clean sheet potential, save points and a low price makes him an excellent option.

Dominik Szoboszlai, Liverpool, midfielder, £7m

Szoboszlai is an intriguing option at £7m after an excellent individual campaign last season. He finished as Liverpool's second highest-scoring FPL player with 160 points - only Virgil van Dijk had more with 175 points.

Liverpool have a very appealing opening five gameweeks, starting with Newcastle followed by Nottingham Forest, Ipswich, Fulham and Bournemouth, and the Hungarian has plenty of routes to points.

He scored 13 goals in all competitions last season, including four direct free-kicks, while also offering assist potential from set-pieces. His impressive work off the ball lead to defensive contribution (defcon) points too.

There are some question marks over exactly where he will play under new Liverpool boss Iraola, particularly with Wirtz likely to slot into the number 10 position. However, Szoboszlai's versatility could actually work in his favour, meaning his minutes should be reasonably guaranteed.

Joao Pedro, Chelsea, striker, £7.5m

The Brazilian is a key pick for our fantasy forward lines, following an impressive debut season for Chelsea, where he racked up 15 goals and nine assists.

He finished the season as the fourth highest-scoring forward in the game, having had 63 shots in the box and 26 big chances on goal.

Having had the summer off, he's well-placed to replicate this output under new boss Xabi Alonso, with Chelsea also having the freedom of no European football to contend with.

He comes in £2m cheaper than Cole Palmer, and as the clear focal point in the Chelsea attack. The only concern is that summer signing Danny Welbeck could compete with him for minutes.

Neco Williams, Nottingham Forest, defender, £5m

The Wales right-back is an intriguing defensive selection for fantasy managers going into this campaign, with a potential change in formation giving him a huge advantage.

We expect to see some defensive solidarity under new manager Oliver Glasner, with this Nottingham Forest side keeping 13 clean sheets in the 2024-25 campaign.

Williams ranked third for fantasy points among Forest players last season, with five goal involvements, leading the way for shots (46) among defenders.

He has the potential to play more advanced this campaign if Glasner adopts his favoured wing-back system, with Daniel Munoz producing eight goal involvements on the left for Palace last season.

Riccardo Calafiori, Arsenal, defender, £5.5m

The Italian doesn't come without risk and Piero Hincapie (£5.5m) is a quality challenger for the left-back position, but Calafiori is a cheap route to the elite Arsenal defence, with Gabriel (£8m) now out of most managers' budgets.

First choice left-back for most of last season, Calafiori's place in the XI feels secure if he can stay fit. Early substitutions are likely but rarely come pre-60 minutes and, with a full pre-season under his belt, many will expect immediate rewards from the attacking-minded full-back who plays for the best defence in the league by some distance.

Cristhian Mosquera (£5.5m) is also expected to start the season with the absence of William Saliba (£6m) but Arsenal have been linked with a centre-back and Saliba's recovery timeline is vague, so Mosquera's run in the team could be short-lived.

title: Dublin Dons? The failed attempt to bring a Premier League club to Ireland
description: Just how close did an Irish consortium come to buying a Premier League team and moving them to Dublin?
fullText:
"People would be laughing now but it's something that would have worked, no doubt about it."

This weekend, and across each one to follow through the Premier League season, thousands will make the journey from all over the island of Ireland to take in a game from England's top flight.

Indeed, despite increased interest in the league from all four corners of the globe, those making the short trip from across the Irish Sea still account for the greatest number of travelling supporters each season.

Such is the fixation with all things Premier League that the 75,000 fans who packed a sold-out Croke Park for last week's friendly between Manchester United and Leeds represented a record crowd for any football match in the Republic of Ireland.

Earlier in the month, Arsenal also drew a huge crowd to the Aviva Stadium for their own friendly with Real Betis.

But what if such occasions were a fortnightly norm rather than summer one-offs? Well, three decades ago an outlandish plan asked that very question.

It started with an innocuous report in a Sunday broadsheet. The newspaper told of Wimbledon chairman Sam Hammam's fractious relationship with Merton Council and the ongoing struggle to come to an arrangement over a permanent home for the club.

Hammam had bought the club in 1981 but, with plans for an all-seater stadium in Merton having come to nothing, they had been ground-sharing with Crystal Palace since 1991, a situation that suited neither landlord nor tenant.

"We'd always get dog's abuse off Palace fans calling us squatters," recalled Kenny Cunningham, the Dublin-born full-back who joined the club from Millwall in 1994.

"There wasn't a huge amount of respect there, I don't think. A bit tongue in cheek maybe, but I think they meant it."

While there were still grumbles over their direct style, the side were undoubtedly effective, finishing sixth in the 1993-94 campaign.

"We were a small team in what was becoming the greatest league in the world. It was a great feeling to be stood in the tunnel, ready to go up against world class players and knowing we had a chance," added Cunningham.

"But there was always the issue with the ground, always the talk about what would happen in the medium to long term. Would they go back to Plough Lane? Would they groundshare?"

Upon reading of Hammam's impasse with the council in the paper, Tommy Higgins landed on a more radical solution.

Through his role with Ticketmaster Ireland Higgins knew that property developer Owen O'Callaghan had planning permission to build a 40,000-seater stadium on the outskirts of Dublin. All the project needed was an anchor tenant. A stadium in need of a club, a club in need of a stadium.

While a first meeting, attended only by Hammam's brother, went nowhere, a chance encounter on the streets of Dublin brought together a heavyweight Irish consortium.

When Higgins and businessman Maurice Cassidy ran into former Republic of Ireland player turned television pundit and journalist Eamon Dunphy along with Paul McGuinness, manager of Irish rock band U2, a decision was made to resurrect the plan.

All knew it was a longshot, but could they pull it off?

The mid-1990s found English football caught between two generations. Edging slowly from the long shadow of the Bradford City Stadium fire, Heysel and the Hillsborough disaster, Roman Abramovich's acquisition of Chelsea heralding an era of foreign ownership was still years away.

While the league was once largely a British and Irish concern, the likes of Jurgen Klinsmann, Dennis Bergkamp and Juninho had sealed incoming transfers to England that would have been unthinkable just a few short years before.

Come 17 August 1996, the opening day of the new season, Gianfranco Zola and Fabrizio Ravanelli were the latest imported stars ready to make unlikely debuts, but it was a considerably more local talent who stole the headlines.

Few goals in Premier League history have been more replayed than David Beckham's audacious lob from the halfway line against Wimbledon at Selhurst Park.

"If you roll it back very slowly to the point of contact where Beckham goes to shoot, you can me see in the far left of the picture," said Cunningham.

"You can blame me for a lot of the goals we conceded when I was at the club, but I don't think I've to hold my hands up on that one.

"But that goal, the way he stepped up on to the scene, there was a lot of commotion about it. That was the Premier League on its way in a lot of ways. It was exciting times."

Among the crowd at Selhurst Park were the Irish consortium, preparing a bid of £6m for 74% of the notional home side.

Following such a public appearance from the key figures involved, it was no surprise when news of the plans soon broke in the media.

"When the story broke at the time people thought it was crazy stuff, a team in Dublin. They couldn't entertain it," said Cunningham.

"Sam Hammam was before his time in terms of thinking about how he could get his club on the back pages. The football took care of Saturday, but from Sunday to Friday, he'd be very astute in that way.

"I remember thinking then was it just another Sam way to generate that bit more publicity around the club and saying to the gaffer 'is there any value in this?' Joe was saying that they were serious."

Cunningham was keenly aware of the interest back home, even if some team-mates were less sure.

"I don't mean it as a criticism, but the English boys were a bit insular maybe," he added. "The lads were talking as if Dublin was the other side of the world, then asking if it was a good night out?

"A good night out in Dublin...are you serious? I was telling them they were going to love it."

Hammam believed that his fellow owners and the league's broadcasters would be no harder to convince than sceptical players. Fans on the other hand...

"I hated it. I thought it was absolutely ridiculous," said Ivor Heller, who had been a Wimbledon supporter since their non-league days in the 1970s.

"From a business point of view, I could see the sense of it. Man United fans, Liverpool fans, Chelsea fans, Tottenham fans, of course they'd all love an away game in Dublin, but for me, it felt like a nightmare.

"Nothing against Dublin, but if we moved there, it was the end of the football club. It could never be Wimbledon in Dublin."

Through his printing business, Heller produced the placards displayed at Selhurst Park which bluntly summed up the mood of the fanbase - 'Dublin = Death'.

The Football Association of Ireland [FAI] were no more enamoured with the project.

While the consortium felt the behemoth of a Premier League club in Dublin would be the rising tide to lift all boats, and Kinnear envisaged a slew of Irish internationals becoming viable transfer targets, the governing body feared it would essentially kill off their own domestic league.

The fan who brought his football club back to life

What if Wimbledon had become the Dublin Dons?

"The concept was really, really strong," said Higgins, now chairman of League of Ireland side Sligo Rovers.

"Jack Charlton's Irish team was in his heyday, and coming off Italia '90 and USA '94, you'd have had a mini-international side playing in Dublin every other week.

"I believe it would have transformed soccer on the island, but they [the FAI] were looking down too narrow a pipe.

"And look at what's happened since - rugby and the GAA have eaten our lunch and they get the money for TV and sponsorship.

"Soccer just didn't have the vision to do something transformative."

In the end, it was a moot point. After 18 months of talks, the line to Hammam went dead. Calls went unanswered, correspondence unreturned.

Higgins, who still has the unsigned contract among his files, was walking through an airport the next year when he looked up at a television screen to see news that Hammam had sold 80% of the club to Bjorn Rune Gjelsten and Kjell Inge Rokke for £26m, more than four times their own bid.

A shopping centre now sits where the Premier League stadium was to be built.

Dublin would not get its team, but nor would Wimbledon keep theirs with the club ultimately moved to Milton Keynes in 2004.

In the community left behind, AFC Wimbledon were born, starting life in the ninth tier of English football that same year with Heller among four co-founders.

Three decades on from those first murmurs of a move to Dublin, the reclaimed club are a League One side and since returned to their spiritual home of Plough Lane.

"You talk about the FA Cup, league finishes, cup semi-finals, but for me what they've done, that's the biggest achievement in the history of the football club," said Cunningham.

"To be knocked for six, to go careening down the leagues, and come back, it's a success every time they take the pitch. Good luck to them.

"The Dublin thing? It's a bit of nostalgia now, maybe a bit of sadness at a missed opportunity.

"People would be laughing now but it's something that would have worked, no doubt about it. Absolutely, people would have rowed in behind it."

title: Strong favourites or tougher task - will Arsenal defend their title?
description: Arsenal begin this season as Premier League champions but just how difficult is it to defend the league title, and how well equipped are they for the challenge?
fullText:
Arsenal ended their long wait to win the Premier League again by securing the title last season.

It means they begin this campaign as defending champions - something they have not done since the 2004-05 season.

The Gunners are favourites to lift the trophy once more - but what does history tell us about how defending champions perform, and just how likely is it that Mikel Arteta's men can claim back-to-back Premier League titles?

Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola made defending the Premier League title look easy in recent years.

After first leading City to the title in 2017-18, Guardiola led a successful defence four times before leaving the club this summer.

But prior to the Catalan's arrival in the Premier League, winning a title two or more seasons in a row was proving a tough task, with the trophy changing hands in each of the eight seasons before Guardiola's first title win.

Before Guardiola there were only two managers who had overseen successful title defences in the Premier League era - Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United and Jose Mourinho at Chelsea.

One of the reasons why it can be so difficult to defend a title is the psychological factor.

For a whole campaign a title-winning team's players have been working hard towards the goal of winning the league and the moment it is achieved will understandably feel like a huge success and relief.

But then, just a few months later, those same players have to build up to the idea of having to do it all again, only this time with a bigger target on their back as defending champions.

That can be overwhelming - as Leicester City found out after their fairytale Premier League win back in 2015-16, when they flirted with relegation in their title defence season.

In the summer after their title triumph, one Foxes player summed up the psychological impact it had on the players, telling the Guardian:, external "Winning the title was like climbing Mount Everest. Then you get back down, receive a pat on the back and you're told to climb up it all over again."

Ex-Premier League winger Andros Townsend believes the Gunners will find it hard to replicate their 2025-26 achievement because of the competitive nature of the Premier League.

"The last two times Liverpool have won the title the next season they have not been able to replicate it. They have had relatively poor seasons," Townsend told BBC Radio 5 Live, with the Reds finishing third and fifth after lifting the Premier League trophy.

"When you get over the line, that huge relief. Do you go into the summer with the same sort of aggression and mentality?"

There have been plenty of changes for Arsenal's title rivals this season.

Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea are going into the campaign with new managers, while Roberto de Zerbi and Michael Carrick will oversee their first full seasons at Tottenham and Manchester United respectively after they were appointed during last season.

That means they will all have a degree of uncertainty in the dugout, while Arsenal have the benefit of continuity as Mikel Arteta remains in charge.

Arsenal have not made too many major changes in the playing squad either, with their significant signings being the arrival of Greece forward Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m, and midfielder Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United for £75m.

Arteta believes the signing of Guimaraes in particular will significantly boost Arsenal's chances of defending their title.

"I think he describes himself as a warrior," Arteta said. "I think he's a warrior with a tremendous quality as well and intuition and leadership and charisma that is going to help us, that is going to really ignite something different in the team.

"We want to go to the next level and are very, very much convinced that we're going to need players with such a personality, desire and character to push everybody inside the organisation to go even higher."

However, Arsenal have been dealt a blow with an injury to defender William Saliba, who is set to miss an "extended period" after suffering a back injury at the World Cup.

His partnership with Gabriel Magalhaes last season gave the Gunners' consistent defensive excellence and, even in light of their attempts to sign Ezri Konsa, how long the France international is out for could have a significant impact.

While managerial changes provide unfamiliarity for some of Arsenal's rivals, it is hard to argue that some of those have every chance of boosting their title chances.

Chelsea, for example, have one of the most sought-after young managers in the game in Xabi Alonso, and also look to have bought well in the transfer market.

Former Liverpool midfielder Alonso, who famously led Bayer Leverkusen to a historic, unbeaten domestic double in the 2023-24 season, appears to have strengthened well, with a mixture of exciting young talent and experienced older heads.

England forward Morgan Rogers, 24, has arrived from Aston Villa for a club record £117m, while France defender Maxence Lacroix, 26, has joined from Crystal Palace for £52m.

Chelsea's new £47m full-back Marco Palestra, 21, has been one of the strongest performers in pre-season, while Premier League winners and veteran figures Jordan Henderson, 36, and Danny Welbeck, 35, have also been brought in to bring a youthful dressing room together and set standards.

Manchester City, now managed by Enzo Maresca following the departure of Guardiola at the end of last season, signed midfielder Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m but appear set to lose Spain midfielder Rodri, who was player of the tournament at this summer's World Cup. However, Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez could be set to replace him.

Manchester United strengthened their midfield while weakening a rival by signing Aston Villa's Youri Tielemans for £35m and also brought in fellow midfielder Andrey Santos from Chelsea for £48m, with the Brazilian having impressed in pre-season.

It is just three months since Villa lifted the Europa League, but much has changed since then with Rogers, Tielemans and Lucas Digne - who all started in the final - having all departed. Key incomings are Johan Manzambi from Freiburg (£59.5m) and Joao Gomes from Wolves for £38m, while Alejandro Garnacho has also arrived on loan from Chelsea.

There have been changes behind the scenes too at Villa, with three coaches having left including set-piece coach Austin MacPhee, who moved to Chelsea.

Liverpool, champions two seasons ago, are now managed by Andoni Iraola and his side should be strengthened by the arrival of centre-back Jeremy Jacquet from Rennes for £60m, while versatile defender Ronald Araujo has joined on loan from Barcelona. The Reds have also brought in 22-year-old forward Victor Munoz, but results in pre-season have been mixed.

Tottenham will expect to be challenging towards the top end of the table after a difficult couple of seasons, and De Zerbi has been working hard to improve his squad, spending well over £200m to bring in Sandro Tonali from Newcastle (£100m), Mateus Fernandes from West Ham (£85m) and Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton (£52m).

Hitting the ground running is always important in a season. While kinder fixtures do not guarantee a strong start, they can certainly help.

Based on global power rankings - which assign an ability score to over 13,500 domestic teams across the world - Opta has ranked the difficulty of every Premier League team's first five games of the season. Of the most probable title contenders, it is Manchester United who Opta ranks as having the most agreeable opening fixtures.

Arsenal and Manchester City were the main players in the title race last season and they have been ranked as having the same level of difficulty for their first set of matches.

The Gunners kick off the season by hosting Coventry, then travel to Aston Villa, followed by Chelsea at home and then Sunderland and Brighton away.

Manchester City, meanwhile, start with a home game against Bournemouth, before travelling to Crystal Palace, hosting Coventry, playing at rivals Manchester United and then facing Sunderland at home.

Community Shield: Reaction as Arsenal cruise to win against poor Man City

title: How important is Community Shield to a team's season?
description: Premier League champions Arsenal take on FA Cup winners Manchester City in Sunday's Community Shield - but would winning suggest a successful season ahead?
fullText:
The Community Shield takes place between two teams who will be hoping to battle it out for the Premier League this season.

English champions Arsenal take on runners-up and FA Cup winners Manchester City at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Sunday.

But do the stats suggest winning the curtain-raiser in the Welsh capital would indicate a successful season ahead? And what of the goalscorers?

Why is the Community Shield being held in Wales?

Considering the current Premier League champions play in the game every season it is surprisingly rare for the Community Shield winners to go on to win the league.

Since the Premier League started in 1992-93, only eight of the 34 winners of the Charity or Community Shield have done so.

Five of those happened in a six-year spell from 2005 until 2010.

Manchester City, in 2019, were the last team to do so - and before that it was Alex Ferguson's Manchester United in 2011.

Only one of the past 15 winners of the Community Shield have gone on to become champions that season.

Since 1992 the teams who lose the Community Shield have won more league titles that season - 10 in total, including Manchester City for three years in a row between 2021 and 2023.

Last year Crystal Palace beat Liverpool and ended up finishing 15th, although they did go on to win the Conference League. The Reds also had a disappointing domestic campaign, finishing fifth.

Some 47% of the time (16/34) the upcoming season's Premier League winners had not been involved in the Community Shield - like Arsenal in 2025-26.

And 53% of the time (18/34) the Shield winners have finished above the losers in the league that season.

On 10 occasions the two teams have finished as the top two in the Premier League - with four of those times being the Shield winners top and the losers as runners-up.

The other question is how many Community Shields are won by the previous season's Premier League winners.

The answer is 18 out of 34 times - so 53%.

But in recent times it has become less frequent. Including Crystal Palace, the FA Cup winners have won eight of the past 12 Shields, something that had only happened five times in the previous 22.

And on three occasions in the Premier League era, neither the league nor cup winners have won it.

Arsenal (1999 and 2023) and Manchester United (2010) qualified as Premier League runners-up and beat the Double winners in the game.

This one is a bit of a mixed bag.

Crystal Palace's 2025 scorers Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr netted 37 goals between them last season.

Hugo Ekitike scored his first of 17 goals in his debut season for Liverpool - but Jeremie Frimpong did not enjoy a great first campaign after netting.

In 2023 Cole Palmer netted for Manchester City in their game against Arsenal (a match they would go on to lose on penalties after Leandro Trossard's injury-time equaliser).

He would go on to score 22 Premier League goals and be named young player of the season... for Chelsea, having joined them for £42.5m.

The previous season, Darwin Nunez scored on his Liverpool debut - and Erling Haaland failed to notch on his City bow.

That led to post-match discussion about Nunez looking the better player.

However, Haaland went on to 52 goals that season, with Nunez netting only 15.

Kelechi Iheanacho only scored four Premier League goals after his 2021 Community Shield winner.

But back in 2019 Raheem Sterling's Shield strike for City against former club Liverpool kick-started the most productive season of his career (31 goals).

title: Premier League clubs looking to EFL for next Semenyo & Eze
description: Premier League clubs are continuing to recruit young players from EFL and Scottish academies for their U21 and B-team squads.
fullText:
When Manchester City paid £12.5m to sign Jeremy Monga from Leicester City last month, they were not alone in wanting one of English football's most highly rated teenagers.

Arsenal also coveted the 17-year-old winger, but City won the battle for a player who joined Leicester aged eight and has already broken records in senior football.

Monga became Leicester's second-youngest Premier League player in April 2025, aged 15 years and 271 days, before becoming their youngest league starter and surpassing Jude Bellingham as the Championship's youngest goalscorer.

He represents the more established end of a wider battle for young domestic talent.

Premier League clubs are increasingly looking to EFL and Scottish academies for players who can be brought into their development structures, sometimes before they have established themselves in senior football.

The appeal is easy to understand.

Antoine Semenyo was rejected by several academies before Bristol City spotted him playing college football. After loans at Newport County and Sunderland, he established himself in the Championship before joining Bournemouth for about £10m, then Manchester City in a £64m move.

Ollie Watkins came through at Exeter City, Adam Wharton at Blackburn Rovers and Eberechi Eze - after being released by Arsenal - rebuilt his career at Millwall and QPR.

For recruitment departments, finding the next player capable of following a similar route can be enormously valuable.

Man City sign Monga - how good is the 17-year-old?

BBC Sport research has identified 14 players recruited from EFL or Scottish Premiership academies for Premier League development squads so far this summer.

That matches the 14 such transfers made across the whole of 2025-26. There were eight in 2024-25, 18 in 2023-24 and seven in 2022-23.

More striking is the profile of this summer's recruits. Of the 14 identified, 11 are 18 years old. Last season only five of the 14 players in the equivalent sample were 18.

League One has also become fertile ground, providing seven of this summer's 14 recruits, compared with just two last season.

Among the youngsters to have moved so far this summer are Blade Earley from Cambridge United to Aston Villa, Valentin Joseph from Blackburn Rovers to Brighton, George Munday from Cambridge United to Brighton, Harrison Bettoni from Wigan Athletic to Chelsea and Maxwell Adedeji from Leicester City to Tottenham.

Monga is not part of BBC Sport's 14-player sample because he had already broken into Leicester's first team. His fee, however, illustrates how quickly the equation can change once a teenager proves himself at senior level.

At 18, players have already received years of professional coaching but remain young enough to spend time in an under-21 or B-team environment before decisions are made over loans or first-team opportunities.

The financial outlay can also be relatively small. Nine of the 14 moves identified this summer are listed as free transfers, with the other five for undisclosed fees. Eight of last season's 14 were also listed as free transfers.

For clubs accustomed to paying tens of millions for established first-team players, spreading comparatively modest sums across several promising teenagers offers obvious appeal. Only one needs to develop into a Premier League regular for the strategy to potentially generate significant value.

The economics of academy recruitment have also become a wider issue. The Premier League has approached the EFL over potentially capping compensation paid when young players move between academies.

Clubs losing youngsters can receive training compensation alongside future appearance-related payments and sell-on entitlements, while unresolved cases can be referred to the Professional Football Compensation Committee.

Before freedom of movement ended, English clubs could scout a vast European market without having to consider whether EU players were eligible to work in the UK.

Analytics FC estimated in a 2022 report, external with immigration specialists Fragomen that about 60,000 professional players in Europe had potentially been available to British clubs before Brexit.

Under the Governing Body Endorsement system it estimated only about 5,000 would be likely to qualify for a permit - a reduction of roughly 92%.

The restrictions are especially relevant to younger players.

Liverpool's Ifeanyi Ndukwe is a good example. The 18-year-old centre-back joined from Austria Vienna and impressed during pre-season but cannot play competitive matches for the Reds because he does not qualify for a work permit. A loan abroad is expected to help him build the experience required to become eligible.

A teenager already progressing through an English academy presents no equivalent immigration obstacle.

Brexit has also affected players moving the other way. Analytics FC found Premier League 2 produced more British transfers to EU clubs than any other English division before Brexit, but those moves had halved by 2021-22.

That does not prove Brexit directly caused Premier League clubs to target EFL academies, but it changed the environment in which young players are recruited and developed.

There is no uniform approach to youth development among Premier League clubs.

International Centre for Sports Studies (CIES) figures for 2025-26 show club-trained players accounted for 16.2% of Manchester City's Premier League minutes, followed by Chelsea on 15.5% and Brighton on 12.5%.

CIES defines a club-trained player as someone registered with their current club for at least three full seasons, or 36 months, between the ages of 15 and 21. That means an 18-year-old recruited from an EFL academy can still go on to qualify as club-trained if he spends the next three seasons with his new Premier League club.

At the other end of the scale, Tottenham's club-trained players accounted for just 0.1% of league minutes, while Bournemouth, Brentford and Burnley were all at zero.

Recruiting from EFL and Scottish academies therefore offers another way of building that development pipeline.

Rather than relying solely on players who have been with a club since childhood, a Premier League side can identify somebody developed elsewhere, bring them into their under-21 structure at 17, 18 or 19 and take responsibility for the final stages of their development.

The numbers do not yet show a relentless increase. There were 18 such moves in 2023-24, meaning this summer's 14 cannot be described as unprecedented.

But the concentration of 18-year-olds and League One players suggests clubs are becoming increasingly precise about the market they are targeting.

For EFL clubs, that raises questions over how long their best youngsters can realistically be retained.

For Premier League clubs, the calculation is different. The next Watkins, Eze, Wharton or Semenyo may already be somewhere further down the pyramid. The challenge is finding them before everybody else does.

title: Can Chelsea go from 10th to title again?
description: With a new manager at the helm in Xabi Alonso, can Chelsea go from 10th to the Premier League title like they did a decade ago?
fullText:
Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League 10 years ago but incredibly were champions of England just a year later under new manager Antonio Conte.

After finishing in the same position last season, with no European football again and a new manager in Xabi Alonso, can the Blues repeat the feat?

Chelsea's Premier League record in 2025-26 is almost identical to when they finished mid-table under interim manager Guus Hiddink a decade ago.

With just one more goal scored and one more conceded, they finished with the same goal difference and just two points more than they did in 2015-16.

Few would have imagined back then that after finishing 31 points behind champions Leicester and below the likes of Southampton, West Ham and Stoke, Chelsea's players would be the ones lifting the Premier League trophy the following season.

After starting the campaign playing a back four, a 3-0 defeat at Arsenal in just their sixth game saw Conte switch his side to a back three. The impact was tremendous as they won their next 13 games in a row.

It's a tactical switch that the Blues could make this season as well under new manager Alonso, given that his Bayer Leverkusen side won the Bundesliga unbeaten in 2023-24 playing three at the back.

That incredible winning run gave Chelsea what proved to be an unassailable lead at the top of the Premier League, as they won 18 games more than in 2015-16 to win the title with 93 points.

Improving the club's points tally by a whopping 43 points again is undoubtedly a huge ask for Alonso's squad, given that it's the biggest points increase that any side has achieved to win the title in Premier League history (Leicester improved by 40 points the previous season).

But they may not need to. While Arsenal will likely mount a stronger title defence than Leicester, the Gunners' points tally last season was the second-lowest to win the Premier League since Claudio Ranieri's side 10 years ago.

The bar to become champions has dropped in the last couple of seasons from the dizzying demands of the Guardiola-Klopp era – where even 97 points wasn't enough in 2018-19 – so Chelsea might not need to reach the 93 that they achieved under Conte.

While Chelsea would still need to improve considerably to win the title, they were better than their lowly 10th-place finish last season suggests.

Based on their underlying expected goal numbers, Chelsea were the fourth-most dominant team in the Premier League (although they drop to fifth once penalties are excluded).

The problem was that Chelsea struggled to take their chances. They scored eight fewer goals than they should have, given the number and quality of shots they took – just 58 from an xG of 66.3 – with only Crystal Palace and Wolves worse finishers than them last season.

Bizarrely, the majority of that xG under-performance in front of goal came in just five games in March and April under Liam Rosenior.

Despite taking 73 shots worth 5.5 xG, the side lost five successive league games without scoring for the first time in 114 years – a run of defeats that saw Rosenior ousted as head coach.

Did Chelsea become bad finishers, was it simply a run of bad luck or was it something else? Whatever the reason, the Blues are unlikely to suffer such a sudden slump again this season.

Given where they finished, the Blues will not be playing in any European competition this campaign. While that's obviously something clubs the size of Chelsea seek to avoid, there are benefits to playing just one game a week.

Since the so-called 'Big Six' – Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Man City, Man Utd and Tottenham – all finished in the top six of the Premier League for the first time in 2010-11, nine of their sides have had no European football to play, with Chelsea and Tottenham set to join that list this season.

All but one have finished higher in the Premier League, with sides moving up five places and taking 16 more points on average than they did the previous season.

While Conte's Chelsea obviously took full advantage by winning the title, Liverpool also came very close to lifting their first Premier League trophy in 2013-14. After finishing seventh the season before, an absence of European football saw them take 23 more points but they ultimately fell just two short behind champions Manchester City.

Manchester United also took advantage of playing once a week last season by taking 29 more points than they did in 2024-25 to finish third, although there was a lot of room for improvement after finishing 15th with just 42 points the season before.

Chelsea's transformation under Antonio Conte was incredible, but there's another title-winning side that can match it – Alonso's Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24.

After taking over as manager in October 2022 with the club in the relegation zone, Alonso led them to a sixth-place finish that season with 50 points – the same tally as Chelsea in both 2015-16 and last season (although Bundesliga sides play four fewer games).

Then in his first full season in charge, Leverkusen incredibly took 40 more points in 2023-24 – just three fewer than Conte's Chelsea did – to win their first-ever Bundesliga title without losing a single game.

Only two sides in Premier League history have finished outside the top three one season and won the title the next – Leicester in 2015-16 and Chelsea a year later – so the Blues repeating such a feat would be remarkable.

But with a team better than they looked last season, the benefit of no European football and a new manager that's already pulled off a miraculous transformation at one of his former clubs, it's certainly not impossible.

title: Tielemans apologises to Villa fans for Man Utd remarks
description: Youri Tielemans apologises to Aston Villa fans after suggesting he had moved to a bigger club in Premier League rivals Manchester United.
fullText:
Youri Tielemans has apologised to Aston Villa fans after suggesting he had moved to a bigger club in Premier League rivals Manchester United.

The Belgium midfielder, 29, moved to Old Trafford this summer on a five-year deal from Villa when United triggered a £35m release clause in his contract.

Tielemans spent three years at Villa Park after joining from Leicester City in 2023, making 134 appearances and scoring 10 goals.

Speaking during United's pre-season tour, Tielemans praised Villa for putting him "back to my best level", before adding: "But there are clubs above Villa, and Manchester United is one of them."

Some Villa fans were unhappy with Tielemans' comments, so he took to Instagram, external to clear the air.

"Never meant for my words in the press yesterday to offend anyone or the institution of Aston Villa Football Club, which I massively respect and I'm grateful for the past 3 years," he wrote on Thursday.

"I must however admit my mistake and apologise for my choice of words, will be more careful in the future.

"Wishing the club the best in the future."

I owe Villa the world but Man Utd are above them - Tielemans

Tielemans, who helped Belgium reach the quarter-finals of the World Cup this summer, signed for United in July until 2031.

Last season he suffered separate calf and ankle problems that restricted him to 35 appearances in all competitions for Villa, the lowest number in a campaign during his time in England.

He called his move to Old Trafford "the culmination of years of dedication since I first fell in love with football" and said signing for "such a special club" like United "feels incredible".

United take on AC Milan and Villa face Borussia Monchengladbach in their final pre-season games on Saturday, before the new Premier League campaign begins next weekend.

fullText:
Chelsea are open to loan offers for Mykhailo Mudryk following his return to competitive action, according to Football London, with Coventry City among the clubs watching developments closely ahead of the transfer deadline.

The 25-year-old has re-entered the picture after disciplinary proceedings were resolved, ending a long period on the sidelines. Mudryk had not featured competitively since November 2024, but he did make brief appearances in Chelsea's final three pre-season matches, a sign that he is back in circulation as the club weighs up the next step.

There is interest from multiple Premier League sides and Coventry's presence in that group stands out. Frank Lampard knows the player from their time together at Stamford Bridge, and that prior relationship could become relevant if Chelsea do decide that a temporary move is the best route for all parties. From Chelsea's side, there is a clear need to balance the player's pathway with a crowded attacking unit.

Xabi Alonso has publicly left the matter open, saying, "No decision made. We need to assess, he is a special player but it is a special case so we need to be sensitive." That line captures the tone around this situation. Chelsea are not rushing, but they are assessing a market in which a loan looks realistic.

Strasbourg also remain a viable solution. Chelsea can still send one more player on loan to their sister club under current FIFA rules, with Genesis Antwi and Filip Jorgensen already moving there. Dastan Satpayev is another name in that conversation, which means there are internal decisions to make over how that final slot is used.

From Coventry's perspective, the attraction is obvious. Mudryk brings top-level experience, speed and unpredictability, and although consistency has often been the question, the talent has never been in doubt. A player of his profile would add a different dimension to Lampard's forward line if a deal became achievable.

Any move would also depend on Chelsea's view of his immediate role. Morgan Rogers has emerged as the leading left-sided option, while Jamie Gittens and Geovany Quenda have both strengthened their cases during pre-season. Pedro Neto can operate on either flank and remains available for the right fee, which leaves competition for places intense.

With three weeks remaining in the window, this feels like a situation moving towards clarity rather than one already decided. Chelsea have options, Coventry have interest and Mudryk has a chance to reset his career with regular football. For now, the key detail is straightforward, a loan is on the table, and Coventry City are firmly in the frame.

As a Coventry fan, this is exactly the sort of report that gets you thinking about what might be possible under Frank Lampard. Mudryk has had a difficult spell, but there is a serious player in there and sometimes a fresh environment is what unlocks everything. If Coventry really are in the mix, then it speaks volumes about the ambition around the club right now.

The biggest reason for encouragement is Lampard himself. He knows the player, knows the personality and will have a clear idea of whether Mudryk could thrive in his system. That matters. Coventry would not be taking a blind gamble here, they would be moving for someone the manager understands.

There is also a footballing upside that is easy to see. Coventry supporters want players who can turn a match in seconds, carry the ball, commit defenders and inject real pace into the attack. Mudryk does all of that. If he arrived with a point to prove, the energy around the CBS Arena would be huge.

Of course, there would be risks. Match sharpness, confidence and expectation would all need careful handling. But on loan, with Chelsea still carrying the long-term picture, this could be the kind of opportunity worth chasing. For Coventry, it would feel bold, exciting and full of upside.

title: 'Same players making the same mistakes' - Howey
description: Newcastle players were making the "same mistakes" in their 3-1 loss to Everton in pre-season on Wednesday, says former Magpies defender Steve Howey.  The Premier League returns next week and Howey believes Matthias Jaissle's side need the time to work on the same issues from last season.  "I was just a little bit disappointed at half-time because it's familiar players - the players that will be making the starting line-up against Liverpool - that are making the same mistakes again," Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle after the match.
fullText:
Newcastle players were making the "same mistakes" in their 3-1 loss to Everton in pre-season on Wednesday, says former Magpies defender Steve Howey.

The Premier League returns next week and Howey believes Matthias Jaissle's side need the time to work on the same issues from last season.

"I was just a little bit disappointed at half-time because it's familiar players - the players that will be making the starting line-up against Liverpool - that are making the same mistakes again," Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle after the match.

"And I'm talking missing chances, even though they might be half-chances and some of them were but some of them were more than half-chances.

"When you've got the ball getting drilled into you, make it stick, but it's bouncing off players, and I'm just thinking we used to see that last season. And I know there's been the World Cup, and you have still got time to work on these things - it's not going to improve straight away, it's going to take time. But it was just annoying because it is the same players making the same mistakes again.

"They'll have a little bit of a breather as such, they'll stretch off and do whatever they have to do, but then go again at the weekend with the two games before getting really ready for the start of the season. Only they'll know individually and collectively if they're ready, but whether they're ready or not, it's coming."
