title: Critical former referees add to culture of fear, says retiring Taylor
description: Retiring Premier League referee Anthony Taylor says his decision to quit was partly due to the toxic debate around officials.
fullText:
Just five weeks ago, Anthony Taylor was centre stage at the World Cup - refereeing the last-16 match between Spain and Portugal in Dallas.

But now, for the first time in 20 years, he is not involved as an English football season gets under way.

From the outside, the turnaround from officiating at the highest level to retirement seems sudden.

Here, for the first time, the 47-year-old explains his decision in detail - opening up on the impact of the often toxic debate surrounding officiating, and the intense scrutiny faced by referees.

Taylor also says he thinks his fellow officials should think twice before criticising their former colleagues in the media and talks of his hopes of helping Turkish football emerge from a sprawling referee betting scandal.

And he reveals what he really thinks of the video assistant referee (VAR) system.

Football Daily - Taylor on retirement, career and scrutiny on referees

Taylor retired last month, announcing in a short statement the end of a career during which he officiated 668 matches in the English professional game, every major domestic cup final, and 163 international fixtures.

He wrote it had been "an immense privilege, but the pressure is intense and the scrutiny is constant".

"It was part of it," Taylor says when we meet at his lawyer's offices in Leeds.

"Any referee will be lying to you if they said that pressure or that scrutiny did not bother them, because that's a natural human reaction.

"One of the challenges that referees face at every level is actually understanding the challenges that we face.

"Fear of making mistakes, external opinion, spectators, managers, parents, media, colleagues. All these things feed into creating self-doubt, lacking confidence, and then things can spiral out of control and you lose the ability to actually have any confidence in what you're doing on the field."

For years, Taylor said he had developed "resilience" to handle the pressures he faced, but can that only last so long?

"Everybody will experience times where dealing with that environment for a long period of time, your energy levels would dip," he says.

"That then starts to impact on motivation and your actual confidence. It goes back to the confidence again of, 'I've got to go again, make sure I don't make a mistake, still want to get to this tournament or have this match'. It's a very real feeling that everybody would go through.

"I was very confident in my own coping mechanisms on how I dealt with that.

"The decision to retire is purely based on my body and my mind coming to its natural course in that current role - and it's ready to go on a new journey."

Having taken charge of three matches in his second World Cup, Taylor says he only decided to retire once his tournament ended, which seemed like "the perfect time".

He says he has not missed gruelling pre-season training drills, but admits to "a hint of sadness" because "that's a big part of my life that I'm going to miss being involved in".

"I wanted to decide when I finished on my own terms," he says. "And I don't think you can say there's any better place to finish than at the World Cup."

So are his family relieved? Last year, Taylor told BBC Sport they no longer went to his matches because of the abuse he received, and spoke about how they were targeted by Roma fans in Budapest Airport after the 2023 Europa League final.

"Undoubtedly one of the things that you are considering are the serious sacrifices that both your family and your friends have made over the years for you to do what you do," he says.

"Family life takes a back seat… so, for sure, that was a big part of why I decided to step back.

"It was in combination with... the scrutiny and the demands placed on referees at the very top level. And that doesn't necessarily mean that you're struggling to cope with those demands, but it comes to a point where it feels that your body and your mind needs to take a break from those kind of pressures."

Taylor has stayed off social media in recent years, but admits there is a limit to avoiding the scrutiny.

"Even away from social media, the general coverage of football these days is 24/7," he says. "So there's a lot more mediums for you to discover what people think about what happened last weekend.

"It's not always negative feedback when you come across fans and people when you're travelling around the country. But it is like you are living in a goldfish bowl for 10 months of the year."

Taylor says the scrutiny on officials is "off the scale", and much of that is from "people in the media looking for things to scrutinise, whether that be fairly or unfairly". He describes it as a "big snowball effect".

Does it disappoint him that includes former match officials?

"Yes, it does personally, because it doesn't have any balance to it a lot of the time," he says.

"It's just part of the focus that comes with football. When we're dealing with supposedly objective analysis of matches, whether that be an expert ex-player in a studio or an ex-referee, that should be balanced and fair.

"If it's all one-sided criticism, that creates a culture of fear, disrespect, shame.

"There's a thirst for people to be told: 'Is the decision right or wrong?' And the reality in football is there's a lot of subjectivity and opinion in the middle of right and wrong. But that's not acceptable a lot of the time now."

Asked if that means he will not go into the media, he adds: "I would never feel like I would be wanting to be in a place where I want to criticise somebody, because I'd like to think I've got a very good understanding of why somebody's made a decision that they've made.

"Of course, a wrong decision can be made. Nobody really chooses to understand the reasoning why.

"I feel my skills and my passion are better suited to trying to pass on that knowledge and experience I've been lucky enough to accumulate over the years."

Asked about allegations of favouritism during the World Cup involving other teams and referees, Taylor said: "It always saddens me when someone's integrity is questioned and they receive threats.

"[The] result of a football match is multifaceted. Of course, referee decisions are part of that, but we have players who have a low passing accuracy. We have players who miss penalties. We have coaches who maybe make the wrong tactical changes or the wrong team selection.

"So there's a huge range of factors that play into a result of the game. So I think it's probably important that people just need to remember that."

Taylor will be trying to pass on his knowledge and experience in Turkey, where he has been appointed director of elite refereeing for the country's football federation.

He will take up that role in the wake of a major refereeing scandal in the country, with a five-year investigation finding 371 of 571 match officials had betting accounts.

Asked how he can help the federation move on, Taylor says: "The main focus, working together with the president and chairman, is on helping the officials - particularly the younger officials in the group - develop, build that resilience, build a better skillset to cope with those demanding matches, and really to drive improvement of standards in that respect and that's the central aim of my role there.

"The role, in a nutshell, is about improving standards for the top-level group of officials in Turkey, along with helping them develop their talent ID programme and also helping their international referees improve, get better, more high-profile appointments. Which is something that excites me.

"I'm very privileged that people hold my experience and knowledge in such high regard that they think I can make such a positive impact.

While Taylor says his biggest regret is never having the chance to take charge of a Champions League final, he relished officiating at his second World Cup, though he found officiating in the extreme heat of Dallas "brutal".

Once again, VAR proved controversial at the tournament, with four new areas covered by the system.

"Anything to do with VAR is good when we're talking about increasing the overall accuracy of decision-making," says Taylor.

"But we also need to remember that VAR is there to create a sense of justice, so [for] the big clear errors, and it's not there for microscopic, long-detail checks. And that's probably where everybody's trying to work even harder to get to, particularly this coming season.

"I think if we continue to focus on not being microscopic and not being too long in checking situations, where we're only using really clear evidence of an error being made, then... yeah, I think people will start to accept and trust the process more."

Asked if it was being used too often, Taylor says: "I think most people agree that does happen on occasions, so it's very sensible for us to say that and acknowledge that sometimes things are taking too long, and we're being too microscopic.

"We don't need to take too long looking at stuff, and we need to act on really clear visual evidence to intervene and change the decision."

title: Fulham leave pitch as Malaga take penalty into empty net
description: Fulham's pre-season friendly against Malaga ends in chaotic fashion as the Premier League side leave the pitch before a penalty shootout.
fullText:
Fulham's pre-season friendly against Malaga ended in bizarre fashion on Wednesday, with the Spaniards taking a penalty into an empty net as Alvaro Arbeloa's side headed down the tunnel.

Malaga equalised in the last minute of normal time, when defender Calvin Bassey was penalised for a handball that allowed Eneko Jauregi to convert from the penalty spot to make it 2-2.

But that was only the start of the chaos.

Former Real Madrid boss Arbeloa was sent off for seemingly remonstrating with the referee at full-time but he headed straight down the tunnel with the rest of his players, who believed that the match was over.

But La Liga side Malaga were expecting a penalty shootout to follow, and remained on the pitch ready to decide the winner of the Costa del Sol Trophy.

With fans awaiting a shootout, striker Jauregi placed the ball on the spot and converted into an empty net before celebrating with his team-mates in front of the home support at Malaga's Estadio La Rosaleda ground in southern Spain.

Fulham maintain both sides agreed the match would end without a shootout should it end in a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

In a post-match report on Malaga's website, the La Liga club wrote: "Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract."

Fulham conclude their pre-season preparations against Stuttgart on Saturday.

title: Can Sunderland defy the Premier League doubters again?
description: Sunderland were one of the stories of the 2025-26 Premier League season - but can they do it again this time around, with added European commitments?
fullText:
Sunderland were one of the stories of the 2025-26 Premier League season.

Promoted from the Championship through the play-offs in May 2025, the Black Cats marked their return to the top flight after an eight-year absence with a remarkable campaign.

Tipped for relegation by many, Sunderland ended the campaign in seventh to qualify for Europe for the first time since 1973.

So why - outside newly promoted teams Hull City, Coventry and Ipswich - are Sunderland once again among the bookmakers' favourites for the drop?

There are three main reasons their doubters can point to: their poor underlying numbers last season, the 'second-season syndrome' for promoted sides and a European campaign to contend with.

But are those reasons justified?

A youngster to watch at each Premier League club this season

Murtagh: 'Second season syndrome is lazy punditry'

While results and where you finish in the table are ultimately all that matter, Sunderland's underlying statistics from last season suggest repeating their success might not be so simple.

Expected goals (xG) tells us how well teams do the basics of creating lots of good chances and limiting their opponents to few low-quality ones, based on how hundreds of teams before them have scored or conceded from those opportunities.

Only relegated Burnley and Wolves had a lower xG difference than Regis le Bris' side last season, while West Ham - with the fourth-worst overall xG - were also relegated.

While Aston Villa and Sunderland made a mockery of xG by finishing much higher in the table, the majority of sides finished mostly in line with their underlying numbers, showing those two overachievers were more the exception that proves the rule.

Indeed, the three sides with the best xG difference finished in the top three in the same order, while - excluding Sunderland - the five sides with the worst made up the bottom five.

Only Man City and Aston Villa overperformed their xG numbers by more than the Black Cats, who scored three more goals and conceded six fewer than expected given the number and quality of shots taken.

So taking the season as a whole, it seems that Sunderland's performances weren't as impressive as their results. But one event significantly affected part of the Black Cats' season: the Africa Cup of Nations.

They were without six players - twice as many as any other side - during the tournament in December and January. While the club's performances had already declined after a strong start, they suffered even more when their squad was stretched.

But once all those players returned, Sunderland's underlying numbers improved throughout the rest of the season and they ended the campaign playing like a mid-table side.

With no Afcon this season, the Black Cats may not suffer such a drop in performance. If they continue the 2026-27 season as they finished the last then relegation should be only a remote possibility.

The belief that promoted sides that stayed up in their first season are often relegated in their second is a popular one, with the phrase 'second-season syndrome' regularly thrown about. But is it as common as people think?

Last season Sunderland and Leeds became the 53rd and 54th promoted sides to survive in the Premier League.

Of the previous 52, only 11 were relegated the following season (21%). The vast majority of promoted teams that stay up do not suffer from second-season syndrome.

However, there is precedent for a promoted side that had a first season as good as Sunderland's to be relegated in their second. In fact, the best promoted side in the 38-game era of the Premier League did just that.

George Burley's Ipswich ended the 2000-01 campaign fifth with 66 points - the highest finish and most points any promoted side has achieved in a 38-game season.

But with European football to contend with, they dropped 13 places and took 30 fewer points the next season as they were relegated in 18th place, with Sunderland the beneficiaries as they finished just one place above them.

Overall, four of the previous 20 promoted sides (20%) that finished in the top half in their first season suffered relegation in their second, with the most recent example being Sheffield United five years ago

The Black Cats were one of the sides that did not as they finished seventh under Peter Reid in 1999-2000 and followed up with another seventh-placed finish a year later (although that position did not bring European football back then).

Sunderland will be playing in Europe this season for the first time in 53 years, with at least eight games in the Europa League on top of their usual domestic commitments.

They are the 10th promoted side in Premier League history to qualify for Europe and just the fifth to do so through their league position, with the others qualifying via cup competitions or fair play.

Despite their squads arguably being the least-prepared to handle the extra fixtures, five of the previous nine teams achieved another top-half finish and just two were relegated - Ipswich in the early 2000s and Hull in the mid-2010s.

Hull were an unusual case as they only finished 16th with 37 points in 2013-14 but qualified for Europe by reaching the FA Cup final.

Their European campaign lasted just four games as they were knocked out in the Europa League qualifying rounds in August and were relegated with 35 points the following May.

But then there is that Ipswich side again.

When Inter Milan knocked them out in the Uefa Cup third round on 6 December 2001, Burley's side had won just one of their first 15 games in the Premier League.

While they did find some form after that - they were 12th with 30 points after 25 games - just one win in their final 13 matches led to relegation.

Sunderland will be hoping to follow the example of the most recent promoted side to qualify for Europe - Wolves in 2019.

Despite playing 17 games as they reached the Europa League quarter-finals in 2019-20, they still had enough in the tank to finish seventh in the league again.

There are definitely the ingredients for Sunderland to have a difficult second season, but given how well-run they have been in their recent rise from League One to Europe, many fans will have faith they will continue to thrive.

title: Newcastle Star Sends Defiant Message Before Premier League Season
description: Newcastle United has entered a dramatically different era this summer, with manager Matthias Jaissle replacing Eddie Howe and several established leaders leaving St. James’ Park in Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon. With last season’s three best players all gone, others within the squad are set to take on greater responsibility. One of them, […]
fullText:
Newcastle United has entered a dramatically different era this summer, with manager Matthias Jaissle replacing Eddie Howe and several established leaders leaving St. James' Park in Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.

With last season's three best players all gone, others within the squad are set to take on greater responsibility. One of them, German defender Malick Thiaw, believes Newcastle should still be targeting European qualification this season, with the potential new captain insisting those departures have not diminished the squad's ambitions.

"I think if you speak about targets, for me personally, of course, to play as the club has used to play in the last three or four years, to play, to fight for Europe, I think that's a target," Thiaw said. "Of course, to be better than last season, to improve, to make the fans happy, to show them that we give everything. I think this is really important, because the fans are a huge part of Newcastle; that's what I experienced in my first year."

Thiaw's comments carry additional weight after Jaissle handed him the captain's armband for Saturday's 2-1 preseason victory over Valencia. The center back played more minutes than any Newcastle player last season and could take on an expanded leadership role following the exits of Guimaraes and Kieran Trippier.

The 25-year-old also believes Newcastle's summer additions, as young as they all are, are already capable of contributing immediately despite their age.

"What I like about the new youngsters, the new generation, they're really confident, that's also how they play," Thiaw said. "So they're not scared to step up, so, yeah, big appreciation to them, they're doing really well, and of course, I think they are still young, you have to give them a little bit of time, but I think a lot of them are already ready to perform, 100 per cent."

With Newcastle having finished 12th in the Premier League last season, Thiaw's European target sounds ambitious at the very least, let alone after losing three of the squad's most important players. Still, the defender believes Jaissle's team has more than enough quality to rebound.

"Of course, the Premier League is always hard, it's never easy, that's what everybody knows," Thiaw said. "But other teams, I know they speak the same about us, so, I'm really, really optimistic as well that we have the quality to perform this season."

There are plenty of reasons to question whether Newcastle can realistically return to Europe immediately after such a disruptive summer, but Thiaw clearly has no intention of lowering expectations.

title: Lampard believes Haji Wright ready for Premier League
description: After struggling to find the field during the World Cup, Wright is ready to lead Coventry into the Premiership.
fullText:
The 2026-27 Premier League season begins next week, and 20 teams enter with dreams renewed for the new year. For Coventry City, who earned promotion to the Premier League after winning the EFL Championship, it will be a chance to compete in the top flight for the first time since the 2000-01 season. And USMNT forward Haji Wright will be a big part of their offense this season.

Wright was one of the major factors behind Coventry's promotion last season, with 18 goals and 2 assists in 40 appearances for the Sky Blues across all competitions. However, he struggled to find any playing time for the USMNT during the 2026 World Cup, with just two minute-long appearances logged for the tournament.

Still, Coventry has relied on him to score goals, and he's done that since he arrived there in August 2023. In 124 total appearances, he's scored 49 goals and added 11 assists. It's that kind of production that head coach Frank Lampard feels has prepared Haji Wright for the rigors of the Premier League.

"When you come into a job, you evaluate the talent in the squad and the need for goals at the top end of the pitch. Haji already had a record as such," Lampard said, speaking exclusively to Stars & Stripes FC. "He was playing on the left wing sometimes under the previous manager, but I felt quite quickly that he's a No. 9 and he prefers to be in that position too. I think it makes the most of his talents and attributes, with his speed, size and ability to run in behind defenses. It will be a big test for him, as with all the players, because there's a big gap with the Premier League. They must be focused on bridging that gap with belief. I think Haji absolutely has the talent to succeed here in the Premier League."

For Lampard, the hope is that Wright is able to continue his goal production to help keep Coventry in the top flight. Most teams that are promoted to the Premier League struggle in that first season, with a big percentage of them getting relegated back to the Championship after one year. Coventry hope to dodge the relegation slide and do what they can to stay afloat. And for Wright, it's a chance to show that he is a dependable striker in one of the best leagues in the world and that he can produce against some of the best defenses on the planet.

Coventry have a tall task ahead of them, as they open up the season on the road on August 21st to defending Premier League champions Arsenal. Three of their first four matches will come against teams that finished in the top 8 in last season's table: Arsenal, Manchester City, and Brighton & Hove Albion. It will truly be a big test for Haji Wright and the Sky Blues as they prepare for their first Premier League season in 25 years.

title: Neto attracting Premier League interest
description: Chelsea winger Pedro Neto has attracted interest from four Premier League clubs, with one believed to be Manchester City.  The 26-year-old Portugal international is not regarded as one of the 'untouchable' players at Stamford Bridge and could therefore move before the transfer deadline.  The club believe the market for wide forwards has been inflated by a lack of options for leading clubs, highlighted by the £117m fee paid for Morgan Rogers and Paris St-Germain's £145m valuation of Bradley Barcola.
fullText:
Chelsea winger Pedro Neto has attracted interest from four Premier League clubs, with one believed to be Manchester City.

The 26-year-old Portugal international is not regarded as one of the 'untouchable' players at Stamford Bridge and could therefore move before the transfer deadline.

However, Chelsea insist they would demand a significant fee for the attacker, who joined from Wolves for £54m in 2024.

The club believe the market for wide forwards has been inflated by a lack of options for leading clubs, highlighted by the £117m fee paid for Morgan Rogers and Paris St-Germain's £145m valuation of Bradley Barcola.

Those figures have influenced Chelsea's valuation of Neto, who is known to be of interest to Manchester City where he would be reunited with former Blues boss Enzo Maresca.

Maresca and Neto are understood to have a strong relationship, and the winger is among those reported to have been frustrated by the Italian's departure midway through last season.

New manager Xabi Alonso has not commented on Neto's future, but he has played the winger in pre-season friendlies, including the 3-0 win over AC Milan on Saturday.

title: Jaissle 'bit scared' how refs will take 'emotional' touchline style
description: Newcastle United head coach Matthias Jaissle cut a measured figure at his unveiling news conference, but Premier League managers will come up against someone very different
fullText:
It was an unveiling that started with a handshake.

But no one needed reminding that Newcastle United head coach Matthias Jaissle might not be quite so friendly in the coming weeks and months.

"Just the first time, guys," he said as he greeted reporters inside the media suite at St James' Park.

Jaissle, wearing a black suit and grey shirt, cut a measured figure throughout his first extended news conference since taking charge of the club earlier this month.

But Premier League managers will come up against someone very different on the touchline.

Those who know Jaissle best even liken the difference between his on and off the field persona to Jekyll and Hyde.

"I will not change my style because that's my personality," the former Al-Ahli and RB Salzburg manager said.

"On the touchline, I am emotional, but I need to respect the box [technical area] a bit more.

"I'm a bit scared. I hope in the beginning the referees can maybe close their eyes here and there a little. I need to learn that.

"I had a long touchline in Saudi Arabia, so I think the GPS would be quite high if I had worn it!"

title: Walker targets instant Burnley top-flight return
description: Burnley defender Kyle Walker warns his team-mates they cannot "have a hangover" as they target an immediate Premier League return.
fullText:
Burnley defender Kyle Walker has warned his team-mates they cannot "have a hangover" after relegation as they target an immediate Premier League return.

The Clarets finished 19th in the top flight last season and begin their Championship campaign on Sunday at home to West Ham, another team relegated in 2025-26.

Burnley have dropped down from the Premier League in 2021-22 and 2023-24, only to then instantly win promotion at the first attempt.

Former England international Walker, 36, feels those at the club cannot feel sorry for themselves if they are to return to the elite.

Speaking at the EFL launch day in Manchester, he said: "I'm very excited, it's a different challenge for me personally but it's all about the club and bouncing back to the Premier League – that is vital.

"This club has had ups and downs, but we need to bounce back and stay in the Premier League for the things this club does for everyone.

"It's about your mentality. The lads have had a taste of the Premier League but we don't want to have a hangover and we want to make sure they are on the ball from the first minute.

"We have an obligation to be - to themselves, their team-mates and also the fans that support this club."

Burnley only won four top-flight games last season, finishing 19 points behind 17th-placed Tottenham.

However, Walker, who won the Premier League six times with Manchester City and also the Champions League, feels there is plenty to be excited about for Clarets supporters.

"At the start of last season we actually did well, we put in a decent run of performances but did not get the points we deserved," Walker said.

"We conceded penalties in the last minute, but that's the cruel world of football, especially in the Premier League, and by the end of it we were a bit far off and we went too many games without getting a win.

"But it is a learning curve for these young players and hopefully they have the fire in their bellies to get back up. Everyone knows what the Championship is like, it is a difficult league and there are going to be expectations for a lot of clubs.

"I'm very excited for it. I was lucky enough to play the first part of the season [on loan] with QPR [in 2010-11] and get a promotion medal.

"But I want to do a full season and do the celebrations and parade at the end of it – and I want to do it with this club, which has a place in my heart."

fullText:
Four-time winners Nottingham Forest will face Leeds in the Carabao Cup in the only all-Premier League tie in the second round of the competition.

Chelsea, who have won the competition five times, will welcome League One Luton to Stamford Bridge, while Tottenham will host Championship side Charlton.

David Moyes will return to Deepdale as Everton visit Preston North End, where he began his managerial career.

Also in the southern section West Ham, who beat Portsmouth in Saturday's first round, travel to fellow Championship side Southampton.

The draw for the second round of the EFL Cup was split across northern and southern sections.

All matches are due to take place in the midweek of the week commencing Monday, 24 August.

The nine English clubs involved in Europe this season will enter the competition in the third round.

Newcastle v West Bromwich Albion

After Sky Sports chose Fulham v Chelsea for live Premier League broadcast on Monday, 24 August, the potential for a knock-on impact was clear.

With the two teams not in Europe, and thus entering the Carabao Cup in the second round, both faced playing two games in the midweek.

Ordinarily, that should mean the EFL Cup ties would be played on the Thursday, with 72 hours' rest.

That, too, would impact the Premier League's weekend schedule.

Fulham's match at Sunderland, which was not selected for TV broadcast, was switched to the Sunday.

Chelsea v Brighton, meanwhile, was chosen by Sky for the Sunday.

That was until both Fulham and Chelsea were drawn at home in the Carabao Cup - and they are not supposed to play at home on the same day. The police will have to make a concession, or the EFL will have to get creative.

But there is another knock-on effect - at very short notice for eight EFL clubs.

The opponents of Fulham and Chelsea - Wimbledon and Luton respectively - are in League One action on the Saturday after the ties.

If one or both Carabao Cup ties are scheduled for the Thursday, then the Saturday games would ordinarily move to the Sunday.

And there's another complication.

The following Tuesday there is a full programme of League One games - and that could impact a further four matches with the potential they might have to move to Wednesday.

title: Championship all-stars to global gamble – will Ipswich's approach work?
description: As Ipswich prepare for their return to the Premier League, BBC Sport look at how they are approaching the transfer market differently.
fullText:
Newly promoted Ipswich Town have quietly been the Premier League's fourth-biggest net spenders so far this summer, behind only Chelsea, Tottenham and Arsenal.

Ten players have joined for a combined £106.6m, but what is most notable about the Tractor Boys' approach under new manager Gary O'Neil is the sea change in recruitment strategy, shaped by lessons learned from their chastening single season in the top flight in 2024-25.

Under O'Neil's popular predecessor Kieran McKenna, who stepped down on 10 June after overseeing three promotions in four full seasons, the Blues targeted players familiar with English football.

McKenna's success was built mainly on players from the UK and Republic of Ireland, supplemented by a handful of overseas additions already accustomed to the language and culture through spells at other English clubs.

Ipswich made 39 permanent first-team signings during McKenna's four-and-a-half-year reign, 32 of them either born or raised in Britain or Ireland, with just two joining directly from European clubs.

But the premium on domestic talent makes it difficult, if not impossible, to bridge the gulf between the Championship and Premier League. The success of Sunderland and Leeds last season demonstrated that for promoted teams to thrive, finding value in the transfer market is essential.

When Ipswich last went up in 2024, 10 of their 12 summer signings were British or Irish players acquired from other English sides.

This time, the Blues have cast their net far wider, with Emersonn and Florentino Luis set to be the first Brazilians to represent the club, Sasa Lukic the first Serbian and Daizen Maeda the first Japanese player.

Of the 10 players purchased, the only Briton is Chuba Akpom from Ajax. Even his arrival is an anomaly, given Ipswich were obliged to buy him following promotion despite an underwhelming loan spell.

New boss O'Neil aims to keep Ipswich in top flight

A youngster to watch at each Premier League club this season

Ipswich's previous recruitment model can be traced back to their four seasons in League One.

After guiding Town back to the Championship in 2023, McKenna admitted the club had made a "conscious decision" not to target overseas players because of the fast and frantic nature of England's third tier.

A largely unchanged – but tightly knit – squad then exceeded expectations by finishing second in the Championship in 2023-24, making Ipswich the first side in 12 years to reach the Premier League through back-to-back promotions.

At that point, the Blues' hierarchy could have ripped up the modus operandi that had served them so well and pivoted towards more extensive overseas recruitment. Instead, they doubled down on the approach, focusing mainly on emerging domestic talent largely unproven beyond the Championship.

A £100m summer spending spree brought Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O'Shea and Jacob Greaves to Portman Road – players who had primarily shone in the second tier but were identified as having the potential to develop into established Premier League performers.

Mindful that the odds were against survival, Ipswich also targeted players thought unlikely to baulk at remaining part of the project in the event of relegation.

McKenna's 'Championship all-stars' fell well short of safety, finishing second bottom with just 22 points, 16 adrift of 17th-placed Tottenham Hotspur.

But once relegation had been confirmed, the Northern Irishman maintained that recruitment had been in the club's "best long-term interests", a view that has arguably since been vindicated.

Despite spending heavily on transfer fees, Ipswich's £77m wage bill was comfortably the Premier League's lowest in 2024-25. That restraint, coupled with a massive boost to TV income and the quick gain made on Delap's move to Chelsea, enabled the club to post a £4m pre-tax profit for the financial year ending in June 2025.

Hutchinson's sale to Nottingham Forest later that summer provided another windfall but O'Shea, Clarke, Greaves and January 2025 arrival Jaden Philogene stuck around to play crucial roles as Town secured an immediate return to the top flight.

This time around, chairman Mark Ashton says Ipswich have to be "a bit braver" in their approach to the Premier League, and the type of players the club are pursuing reflects that increased ambition.

Japanese attacker Maeda and Morocco centre-back Issa Diop were both on target at the World Cup this summer, and a third goalscorer from that tournament could follow.

The Tractor Boys have been linked with a move for Paraguayan forward Julio Enciso, who played under O'Neil at Strasbourg last season and had an injury-blighted loan spell at Portman Road during the second half of 2024-25.

While McKenna had enough credit in the bank to play the long game, O'Neil knows he needs to forge a competitive side quickly.

"Two seasons ago, the club didn't get anywhere near staying in the division and this time we need to do better," he said last month. "That's why we're trying to add quality to the squad from different parts of the world and we're trying to add some different attributes."

The former Bournemouth and Wolves boss indicated after Saturday's 3-0 win against Rayo Vallecano that more incomings are likely, saying the "plan is to do quite a bit more".

Ashton acknowledges that one of the key lessons from their previous Premier League campaign was the need to bring in more athletic players "with a different set of physical attributes".

The midfield lacked power and ball-winning ability in 2024-25, and it is imperative that new arrivals Florentino Luis and Sasa Lukic – both experienced at the highest level – hit the ground running. That will be especially important with last season's mainstays Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor doubtful for the opening game following operations over the summer.

It is no surprise that O'Neil is also seeking greater cutting edge given that no Ipswich player scored more than 10 non-penalty goals in the Championship last season.

The Blues broke their transfer record to sign Brazilian striker Emersonn, 22, for an initial £24m. He certainly fits the desired physical profile but is relatively raw, having only established himself as a regular last season at Toulouse, where he scored seven goals in 31 appearances, 22 of them starts.

Maeda, a hardworking forward or winger, had an excellent record at Celtic, netting 79 times in 212 games, but won't get the same volume of chances in a team battling to stay up.

The Suffolk side have also recruited two Dutch goalkeepers, including Kjell Scherpen, whose imposing 6ft 9in (2.06m) frame means he is set to become the tallest player to appear in the Premier League.

With a new manager in place and a £30m training ground redevelopment close to completion, this could be a defining summer for Ipswich. But will their transfer business be enough to secure successive top-flight campaigns for the first time in a quarter of a century?

Only three promoted clubs have splashed out more in a summer window – Sunderland in 2025, Nottingham Forest in 2022 and Aston Villa in 2019 – and all survived.

Yet Fulham, Southampton, Burnley and Ipswich themselves have spent comparable figures in recent years only to swiftly return to the Championship - with that level of investment increasingly the bare minimum needed to be competitive rather than a guarantee of safety.

fullText:
The influence of new manager Alvaro Arbeloa has been evident in Fulham's transfer strategy this summer, with the former Real Madrid bringing in the likes of Gonzalo Garcia and Cesar Palacios.

Arbeloa continues to scour the market for more Spanish talents as he looks to kickstart a new era at Craven Cottage.

Hector Fort has no future at Barcelona. (Photo by Clive Brunskill/Getty Images)

Arbeloa's search has now led him to Barcelona, with Fulham eyeing a move for the club's defensive prodigy Hector Fort, reports Diario SPORT.

According to the report, Arbeloa is on the hunt for a right-back and has asked Fulham to sound out the economic conditions required to lure Fort to the Premier League.

Fulham are not the only English club keen either, with several outlets insisting Everton also retain an interest in the Barcelona academy graduate.

Fort, who is valued at around €10 million, could therefore have no shortage of options should he decide his future lies away from Camp Nou.

The full-back currently continues to train under Hansi Flick, but his long-term prospects at the club appear uncertain.

Hector Fort likely to fall behind Espart in the pecking order. (Photo by Alex Grimm/Getty Images)

Fort is considered one of the candidates to leave in the final stretch of the window in search of regular minutes.

He already spent last season on loan at Elche, where he recovered from a serious injury to finish the campaign strongly, and another temporary or permanent move could now be on the cards.

The right-back position at Barcelona looks well stocked. The continuity of Jules Kounde, combined with the expected permanent return of Joao Cancelo from Al Hilal, suggests Fort may struggle for opportunities.

Not to mention, coach Hansi Flick is extremely happy with the progress of Xavi Espart, who might even move ahead of Fort in the pecking order.

For Fort, a switch to Fulham would represent an exciting opportunity to test himself in the Premier League under a coach clearly willing to trust young players.

He featured in all eight games and was awarded the tournament's Golden Ball for his impressive performances.

Rodri has been a crucial first-team member for Man City since joining them from Atletico Madrid in 2019.

Given his huge importance, Man City are reluctant to part ways with the midfielder.

But Rodri's contract at the Etihad Stadium will expire in June 2027 and he has made it clear he doesn't want to renew his deal.

title: ‘Time is the key, they are young lads’ Matthias Jaissle reflects on first win ahead of huge season ahead
description: Matthias Jaissle saw his Newcastle United team win at their first attempt, against Valencia. Only a friendly of course but so important for NUFC to start building some momentum and confidence with the Premier League season only two weeks away now.
fullText:
Matthias Jaissle saw his Newcastle United team win at their first attempt, against Valencia.

Only a friendly of course but so important for NUFC to start building some momentum and confidence with the Premier League season only two weeks away now.

With Matthias Jaissle thrown in the deep end and such a turnover in the Newcastle United squad, so important for the new boss to see encouraging signs he can build on.

Going behind after only four minutes away from home against a team who finished top half of La Liga, no doubt plenty of Newcastle United fans feared the worst.

However, the Matthias Jaissle era saw the team show plenty of character to bounce back and win 2-1 with two second half goals from Yoane Wissa. Indeed, United could have been ahead by the break as Elanga had a goal disallowed that replays suggest wasn't offside and then Osula denied what looked a clear penalty.

Reflecting on the match and result Matthias Jaissle wanting to keep everybody grounded:*"We will not smash the locker room down and celebrate a lot, we are quite balanced. We know what this is about, it is pre-season and we still have a lot to do. We don't want to hang victories higher than they are and we also don't want to place losses lower than they should be. Next week there are things that we need to work on definitely but we did well in the camp [at La Manga] and in this friendly win."*

A ridiculous challenge/assault by Gaya on 35 minutes saw Anthony Elanga stretchered off and the Valencia captain sent off.

Everybody fearing a needless serious injury in a friendly but reassuring words from Matthias Jaissle: *"It was a shocking challenge and I was in fear [it was a serious injury], definitely. But now I'm more relaxed because the medical department are almost showing green lights that it is nothing serious. We are blessed. Hopefully he can be back in the next week. Anthony seems to be okay, that's the most important thing, that there is no serious injury as it looks right now."*

Matthias Jaissle talking more about the team performance: "Winning games always helps to gain confidence and we also knew that we had a hard week behind us. The players did well and there was a huge commitment in each session, so they really deserve two days off and then we start again. Time is the key, they are young lads. It's never going to be easy in football, especially at the highest level, but we're here to do that."

Nick Pope was part of the week's training camp but missing from the matchday squad against Valencia. Now that Lukas Hornicek has arrived and Ewen Jaouen as cover, it is expected now that Nick Pope will be allowed to move on.

Matthias Jaissle commenting on the NUFC keeper: *"I had a talk with Nick. I really appreciate what he did in his career so far, [but] he knows exactly the situation right now and we need to deal with it in the best possible way. But I always appreciate the player and the human being behind."*

title: Garcia hopes long-term friend Alonso's Chelsea finish second to Liverpool
description: As two Liverpool legends meet in pre-season, Luis Garcia says he hopes Xabi Alonso's Chelsea finish behind their former club in the Premier League.
fullText:
When Chelsea arrive in Malaysia for the final leg of their pre-season tour, new manager Xabi Alonso will be reunited with former Liverpool team-mate Luis Garcia.

Garcia is now the chief executive of Johor Darul Ta'zim, who welcome Chelsea to their 40,000-capacity Sultan Ibrahim Stadium on Sunday.

The two Spaniards go way back to 2004, when they both signed for Rafael Benitez's Liverpool on the same day.

Despite facing each other multiple times in the Spanish football ecosystem, that day at Anfield was the first time they met properly.

"He told me he didn't speak English too well before our unveiling press conference," Garcia told BBC Sport.

"I answered the first question in Spanish, as we had a translator present, and he answered in perfect English and I thought: 'Why you little?!'"

Both started in Liverpool's dramatic Champions League final win over AC Milan at the end of that season and they went on to play together for Spain.

Garcia says they remain "really good friends" and have stayed in touch, but insists Alonso is facing a difficult final overseas friendly.

After matches in Australia and other parts of Asia against elite European football opposition such as Tottenham, Juventus and AC Milan, Chelsea's tour ends in Johor.

The match will be a monumental moment in the JDT's history and for Malaysian football as a whole.

"Chelsea is the biggest test we will face this season," Garcia admits. "I'll be so happy to welcome them in Johor. The stadium is going to be packed.

"We can't wait to challenge ourselves against a top club, top players and it is great to face Alonso. I can assure you on Sunday we will compete.

"I wish him all the best [at Chelsea], but even though I love him, hopefully he ends up second to Liverpool next season."

Joao Pedro scores twice as Chelsea brush aside AC Milan

JDT drew with Rangers and Spanish second-division side Elche before beating Cartagena, as they took on European opposition in a training camp in Alicante.

They have not lost a domestic match since 2021 and are currently on a world record-equalling 108-game unbeaten run, which could soon be extended when the Malaysian season restarts in August.

Success on the Asian continent is also becoming a realistic prospect after reaching the quarter-finals of the AFC Champions League last season.

"Hopefully in the first game of the season we'll break one of the most incredible records in football, that is the domestic unbeaten run," Garcia said.

"The owner is the Crown Prince, His Royal Highness Ismail Tunku. He has taken the club on an amazing journey. Top-class stadium and training facilities that people will be talking about.

"We don't have a limit, and that motto of 'the sky is never the limit' is something that we repeat quite often in the dressing room."

Those facilities are based on Real Madrid's aptly nicknamed White House training base.

Garcia, who splits his time between Spain and Malaysia, gained his Uefa Pro Licence and sporting director licence after retiring.

However, his work also extends to commercial activities and wider planning behind the scenes, although he leaves the coaching duties to compatriot Xisco Munoz.

There are also Spanish coaches throughout the backroom staff and academy, delivering best-in-class coaching to Malaysian talent.

"We want to increase the level of Malaysian football and have a fantastic academy. We brought Spanish coaches to the academy so we can get closer to the best, professional style of work," Garcia added.

"Spain winning the World Cup shows you the value of having a coaching programme and a football philosophy that lasts 25-30 years.

"We got to the quarter-finals of the Asian Champions League and would like more Malaysian teams in the competition.

"The next step is to compete in the Asian Champions League and last year was our main introduction. We arrived there, and we kind of caught up with the situation. It was difficult against teams that [have] got budgets that pass over $150m (£111.2m) and we only have $15m, so it's quite a difference, a big gap between.

"But we want to contribute to the development of Malaysian football to reach the World Cup some day."

title: Arsenal sign Guimaraes from Newcastle in £75m deal
description: Premier League champions Arsenal sign Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United for £75m.
fullText:
Arsenal have signed Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United for £75m.

The former Newcastle captain made it clear he wanted to join the Premier League champions earlier this summer.

The 28-year-old Brazil midfielder, who has signed a four-year deal with the option of a further 12 months, called the move one of the "toughest decisions" of his life.

"This move is very tough because Newcastle means so much to me," he added.

"But I wanted to experience something new in my life. I feel ready for a new challenge for myself and my family."

Newcastle said they wished Guimaraes and his family well.

Guimaraes left Newcastle's training camp in La Manga in Spain earlier this week to finalise his move to Emirates Stadium following a breakthrough in talks.

He revealed he received messages from a number of his future team-mates, including countryman Gabriel as well as fellow midfielder Declan Rice.

Following their previous battles in the middle of the park, Rice told him "come here and please no more fights, now we're friends".

"I'm at the point of my life, I think I need a challenge like this," Guimaraes said.

"I want to win trophies, I want to make history and I think I'm in the right place to do it. I'm so excited to start."

Guimaraes joined a Newcastle side in relegation trouble in January 2022 and went on to play a crucial role in their improvement in fortunes under former head coach Eddie Howe.

The Brazilian became the first captain in seven decades to lift a major domestic trophy for Newcastle after they defeated Liverpool in the 2025 EFL Cup final.

He was also part of the side who qualified for the Champions League in 2023 and 2025, before they slipped to 12th place in the Premier League last season.

Defending champions Arsenal will look to win their first-ever back-to-back Premier League titles, while Manchester City, Chelsea, and Liverpool — all under new management — are expected to challenge for the prize.

description: Premier League newcomers Coventry City have completed the club-record signing of Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi.
fullText:
Premier League newcomers Coventry City have completed the club-record signing of Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi.

The 20-year-old has signed a long-term contract, with the Sky Blues believed to have paid Danish side Nordsjaelland a fee of 27m euros (£23.1m), plus 3m euros (£2.5m) in add-ons.

Yirenkyi made his international debut in May 2025 and played at this summer's World Cup, scoring a stoppage-time winner in the Black Stars' group win over Panama.

He becomes Coventry's fifth summer signing after Frank Lampard led the club back into the top flight after a 25-year absence.

"When I spoke to the head coach about the plans and the style, it's something I really like, and I look forward to learning from him," said Yirenkyi.

"I'm still young so I want to learn from the head coach, the other players and work really hard for the team."

He is a product of the Right to Dream academy and joined Nordsjaelland in 2024, winning the Danish Superliga's young player of the year award last season.

Although primarily a midfielder, Yirenkyi is known for his versatility having played at right-back for both club and country.

Danish journalist Nicklas Degn, who hosts the Mediano podcast, said Yirenkyi is an "extremely exciting player" who has been "touted as the next big thing".

Speaking to BBC Sport, he added: "He's been one of the best players in the Danish Superliga in the past season and he's extremely highly regarded.

"Everyone knew it would just be a matter of time before he went to a bigger league, especially after his World Cup.

"There's always a big focus on the young talents of Nordsjaelland. They are a club that has an academy with a talent development that has an extremely high reputation internationally.

"He's a complete number eight but his versatility is underscored by the fact he's been playing in defence for much of the spring at both Nordsjaelland and for the Ghana national team.

"Coventry will be getting their hands on a extremely exciting player who plays with a maturity well above his age group."

title: A secret invite and other 'pinch-me' moments before Leicester woke up
description: Leicester are gearing up for League One but 10 years ago they were defending Premier League champions. The dream moments haven't been forgotten.
fullText:
It was a dream then, it is a dream now - especially as Leicester prepare for League One.

Ten years ago the Foxes were preparing to defend their Premier League title and looking forward to Champions League football.

At 5,000-1, they had pulled off the most improbable, the most stunning, the most incredible feat to shock the world.

But now, after back-to-back relegations, those days seem almost as surreal as when they actually happened.

New manager Russell Martin will be expected to take the club back to the Championship at the first attempt, something that sounds nowhere near as impossible as what the Foxes previously managed.

A decade on, the 'pinch-me' moments live on for those who were there, and some have shared them with BBC Sport.

Spoiler: they might not be the ones you knew about.

Leicester had won the title without kicking a ball on 2 May 2016 when nearest challengers Tottenham Hotspur could only manage a 2-2 draw with Chelsea.

The next day, there was only one group of men the media wanted to speak to.

The trouble was they were hard to find.

Crowds gathered at the club's former training ground at Belvoir Drive, a few miles outside the centre of Leicester.

Journalists and fans waited - one cameraman persuaded a neighbour to allow him in to film from their bathroom window as he aimed to get footage of the celebrating Foxes.

The media were finally instructed to head to King Power Stadium where the press room would be opened.

A five-minute drive took 30 minutes through revelling fans and it was a battle to get to there but, inside, the world's media edged in, hoping to hear from those who made this miracle possible.

But only eight reporters would receive a secret invitation to head back to Belvoir Drive.

Quietly, one-by-one, the handpicked members of the British press who regularly covered the club, slipped out of the packed room and made their way back.

This time, they were let in and ushered into the family room, just to the right of reception.

When manager Claudio Ranieri walked in, he received an immediate, impromptu, standing ovation and shook hands with those who had watched the astounding season unfold.

The man the world wanted to speak to gave an engaging audience to a few writers for 45 minutes.

Ranieri had been a left-field appointment at the start of that season, having not managed in England for 12 years since leaving Chelsea in 2004.

And he had considered bringing in some unconventional methods, such as double training sessions, which were nipped in the bud with the help of Craig Shakespeare, who had stayed on as assistant after the sacking of Ranieri's predecessor Nigel Pearson.

There were off-field changes he would bring in, though, including taking the squad out to make their own pizza after the first clean sheet of the season against Crystal Palace in October 2015.

"It sounds funny - we're keeping a clean sheet and gone for pizza but you then end up speaking to someone in the squad you probably wouldn't have spoken to at training because there's 25 of you," says former centre-back Robert Huth.

"You train, but you don't really know the guy. How's he functioning? Does he like me to shout at him? Does he want me to just be quiet?

"You talk and go through the game where maybe you wouldn't mention things, like a problem that you see on a pitch, if it's like, a stiff environment.

"If you're out and about, and you go: 'When the ball's here, I prefer if you do this' - just like tiny little things and you take criticism on differently when you talk in a social environment. You don't want to sit in a meeting room being told what to do."

It allowed winger Riyad Mahrez to flourish and Jamie Vardy to plunder 24 league goals, with Ranieri comparing his counter-attacking forwards to the RAF.

It is well documented that Vardy had invited the squad to his house to watch what would end up being the title-winning match as Spurs blew a 2-0 lead to draw with Chelsea - and that some players needed to wait at the local police station before arriving because of the crowds of fans who had gathered outside.

But not all his team-mates were there.

While everyone else partied, winger Nathan Dyer had a different night, in hospital with wife Laura after the birth of their second child, Shea, two days earlier.

"I had the laptop out watching the game in hospital, the boys were at the party. I wasn't able to make it but I'd never miss the birth of my child," he says.

"It was a strange feeling. It was surreal, like it wasn't real at the time but it was.

"We had to be put in a room as people were putting their heads round and even then you could see the eyes at the door. People were congratulating me and were really proud.

"It was the whole city, even people who were not fans were so happy Leicester had achieved this."

He'd had a dramatic arrival at the club in the first place that season, joining on loan from Swansea on transfer deadline day and being flown to Leicester in the late former owner Khun Vichai's helicopter to beat the deadline.

"My wife was pregnant, we'd just moved into a new house, so everything was in boxes, it was a wild day," he says.

"It was exciting for me but also nerve-wracking because it was so intense, to send the helicopter to get me to get it over the line. It was a proud moment for me - I'd always wanted to be involved in a moment like that, watching on the TV - breaking news!"

Leicester were two points behind Arsenal at the turn of the year but one defeat in the final 16 games - a dramatic late loss at Arsenal in February - had put them on course for the title.

The closer they edged to the impossible, the more the interest in the Foxes exploded.

Vardy had a lookalike - postman Lee Chapman - and Ranieri had a sausage named after him.

Local butchers W Archer & Son created the Ranieri from Packington free-range pork, fennel, garlic and chilli.

It won a star at the Great Taste awards and at one stage the shop was shifting 12kg (26.5lb) a day.

Owner Sean Jeynes even brought a plate of sausages to the stadium before a news conference, which led Ranieri to declare himself 'the sausageman'.

"It was surreal that day. How did that ever happen?" says Jeynes.

"We were making sausages two or three times a day, smelling of garlic, smelling of fennel, but it was just a crazy time. It really was a crazy time - you can't quite comprehend what it was like.

"It had a massive effect on the city, it had a great effect on everybody. Everyone was much happier.

"Nothing can replace the Italian sausage, the recipe, and the pork, fennel, garlic chili and a hint of Champions League.

"People would say, why don't you do a [Brendan] Rodgers sausage [after winning the FA Cup in 2021], but it's just not the same."

The sausage is still occasionally back on their counters, a lasting reminder of a unique time.

That is not the only taste of success that is still being enjoyed today.

"Thanks to Leicester City it meant I could retire at 55 instead of 67," says Foxes Trust co-chair Lynn Wyeth, who stuck £2 on the club at odds of 5,000-1 at the start of the season.

"It was actually really stressful. A first world problem, isn't it? It was stressful enough, watching them get closer and closer thinking, oh my god, can we do it? But knowing that there was £10,000 riding on it as well, was like, 'oh, no, I almost wish I'd cashed out earlier'.

"When I won, I had my account shut for money laundering, I had to prove it was me and that I'd won it.

"We managed to clear it up quite quickly, I think it's just an automatic thing.

"There you go. Thank you, Leicester."

title: Why can't the Premier League attract the world's best players?
description: Vinicius Jr chose to stay at Real Madrid, but why does the Premier League rarely attract global superstars at their peak?
fullText:
Had Vinicius Jr joined Arsenal, he would have been a rarity as a genuine global superstar moving to the Premier League at the height of his powers.

The Gunners were prepared to make the Brazil forward their primary target should he decide to leave Real Madrid, and the 26-year-old was open to the possibility.

But he has now signed a new contract at the Bernabeu until 2032.

It is another reminder of a curious contradiction.

Premier League clubs have unrivalled collective spending power and England's top flight is widely regarded as the strongest domestic competition in world football, but attracting established Ballon d'Or contenders has proved difficult.

They have little problem attracting and retaining elite centre-backs and goalkeepers but the scarcity is more obvious further forward, where the most coveted attackers and attacking midfielders still often choose elsewhere.

Since the Premier League began in 1992, only three players have won the men's Ballon d'Or while representing an English top-flight club: Liverpool's Michael Owen in 2001, Manchester United's Cristiano Ronaldo in 2008 and Manchester City's Rodri in 2024.

What England has been exceptionally good at is providing the environment in which elite talents become global stars.

Dennis Bergkamp arrived at Arsenal after a difficult spell at Inter Milan and became one of the Premier League's most influential players. Eric Cantona had already shown flashes of his talent in France and at Leeds before becoming the emblem of Manchester United's first great Premier League side.

Thierry Henry arrived in north London after an underwhelming spell at Juventus before developing into one of his generation's outstanding forwards. Ronaldo joined United as an exciting 18-year-old from Sporting, won the Ballon d'Or five years later, then signed for Real Madrid the following summer.

Erling Haaland is perhaps the clearest recent example. Already one of Europe's most coveted young forwards when Manchester City signed him from Borussia Dortmund in 2022, Haaland had yet to reach the level he has in England.

That is different from signing a player such as Vinicius after he has already won multiple Champions Leagues and established himself among the world's most recognisable footballers.

There have been exceptions, but many of the biggest names arrived after their peak.

The clearest comparison to Vinicius is Andriy Shevchenko, who joined Chelsea from AC Milan in 2006 at the age of 29. He had won the Ballon d'Or only two years earlier and finished fifth in 2005, making him one of the rare established global superstars to move to the Premier League while still close to the height of his career.

Other Ballon d'Or winners such as Ruud Gullit and George Weah also joined Chelsea, but later in their careers, while Ronaldo returned to United at 36, Zlatan Ibrahimovic arrived at 34, and Jurgen Klinsmann signed for Tottenham at 30.

During the 1980s and 1990s, Serie A was both enormously wealthy and the undisputed home of football's biggest stars.

Diego Maradona left Barcelona for Napoli. Brazil's Ronaldo moved from Barcelona to Inter at his explosive peak. Michel Platini, Marco van Basten, Lothar Matthaus and Zinedine Zidane all spent some of the finest years of their careers in Italy.

But the Premier League's financial dominance has produced a different transfer market.

English clubs spend enormous sums, but it can be distributed across deep squads or on players already proven within the competition.

Alexander Isak, Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson, Moises Caicedo, Declan Rice and Jack Grealish have all moved between Premier League clubs for more than £100m.

Others, such as Liverpool's Florian Wirtz, arrive from overseas with enormous reputations but with their best years potentially still ahead.

The model is less about importing one 'Galactico' and more about assembling 18-22 elite players capable of surviving a demanding season.

Real Madrid and Barcelona are difficult for English clubs to compete with when the world's most coveted players become available.

Jude Bellingham is a striking example. Having left Birmingham City for Borussia Dortmund to continue his development, the England midfielder moved to Real Madrid rather than back to his home country.

He remains the only player to represent England's senior men's team during the Premier League era without making an appearance in the competition.

Kylian Mbappe was linked with several clubs elsewhere before fulfilling his ambition of joining Real Madrid, while Neymar chose Barcelona over interest from Premier League teams when leaving Santos in 2013 - attracted in part by the chance to play alongside Lionel Messi.

Cristiano Ronaldo left Manchester United for Real Madrid a year after winning the Ballon d'Or, while Luis Suarez joined Barcelona months after winning the Premier League Golden Boot and PFA Players' Player of the Year with Liverpool.

And Gareth Bale and Eden Hazard swapped London for Madrid after establishing themselves among the Premier League's leading players. Bale joined Real from Tottenham in 2013 after winning the PFA Players' Player of the Year award for a second time, while Hazard made the same move from Chelsea six years later, having previously won the league's top individual honour.

Harry Kane later departed Tottenham for Bayern Munich despite sitting only 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's Premier League record of 260.

There are practical attractions to Spain - climate, lifestyle and, for many South American players, linguistic and cultural familiarity - but the appeal runs deeper.

Real Madrid and Barcelona carry a particular status as destination clubs, reinforced by their Champions League history, global reach and association with individual honours such as the Ballon d'Or.

Both have been interested in Rodri this summer.

Man City reject Barcelona's £38.5m bid for Rodri

Barcelona? Real Madrid? Man City's Rodri has a decision to make

Haaland, meanwhile, represents the counterargument. City signed him from Dortmund at 21 and he has developed into one of the world's most feared number nines.

But even his future illustrates the enduring pull of Real Madrid.

Speaking to DAZN during the 2026 World Cup, Haaland's father Alfie was asked about the prospect of the striker one day moving to the Bernabeu.

"He's happy at City, he's got a long contract… but any player wants to play for Real Madrid," he said.

That does not mean a move is imminent, but the sentiment is revealing. England has repeatedly shown it can provide the stage on which superstars are made. Persuading those already at the summit to choose the Premier League - and convincing those who reach it there to stay - remains the harder task.

title: Journalist: Liverpool Not Interested In Premier League Defender
description: Djed Spence Transfer Talk Leaves Liverpool Still Searching for Defensive BalanceLiverpool’s summer has acquired a familiar shape, one in which need is obvious, solutions appear briefly within reach,...
fullText:
Liverpool's summer has acquired a familiar shape, one in which need is obvious, solutions appear briefly within reach, and then recede just as quickly. The latest example is Alex Crook reporting that the club are not pursuing Djed Spence, despite the logic of the move appearing relatively straightforward from the outside.

Spence, at 25 and an England international, seemed to fit several of Liverpool's more immediate concerns. He offers cover at right back, where uncertainty remains, and can also operate on the left, a versatility that often becomes more valuable the deeper a season goes. In a squad with clear homegrown pressures and visible structural gaps, the appeal was easy to understand. At around £35m, the numbers looked manageable, too.

That is what makes this update feel significant. A sensible transfer is not always the right one, of course, but in Liverpool's current circumstances practicality ought to have some value. Modern squad-building is often described in the language of elite recruitment and market opportunities, yet title challenges are usually sustained by accumulation, by filling weak points before they become fractures.

There is a tactical dimension to this beyond mere depth. Liverpool are entering a new era under Andoni Iraola, and any head coach inheriting a side in transition requires players capable of absorbing varied demands. Full-backs, in particular, are no longer simple touchline runners. They are pressure valves, build-up options and defensive stabilisers. A player able to function on both flanks has obvious value in that context.

Even if Liverpool believe Conor Bradley can reclaim the right-back role, the season demands more than faith. Availability matters as much as talent. Jeremie Frimpong brings qualities of his own, though defensive security has hardly ceased to be a discussion point. On the opposite flank, depth is similarly open to question.

And this is where transfer windows are judged, not by the drama they generate but by the order they impose. Liverpool need reinforcement in defence, and perhaps beyond it. A centre-back, midfield support and attacking depth all have their place in the conversation, but the immediate sense is of a squad still awaiting basic repair work.

Spence may not have been the perfect answer. He may not even have been the preferred one. Yet if Liverpool decline that sort of solution, then what follows has to be persuasive, because the season is close and the margins at the top of English football are ruthlessly narrow.

From a Liverpool perspective, this report lands with a weary sort of familiarity. Djed Spence was never the sort of signing to set pulses racing, but that may have been precisely the point. Supporters can live without spectacle in the market if the squad starts to make more sense. Right now, it still does not fully make sense.

There is always the possibility that the club have a better plan. Recruitment departments do not, in fairness, operate according to public logic alone. They may see flaws in Spence's profile, or believe the money is better deployed elsewhere. If so, fine. But Liverpool have drifted into that dangerous territory where every sensible missed opportunity sharpens attention on what has not yet been fixed.

An unsure fan would probably say this is less about Spence himself and more about confidence in the process. If Liverpool pass on a player who looks useful, adaptable and reasonably priced, then supporters need to see the alternative quite quickly. Otherwise, the fear grows that obvious needs are being left to harden into recurring problems.

There is enough quality in the squad to compete, and Iraola is walking into a group with serious talent. But talent needs structure around it. At the moment, the concern is that Liverpool still look one or two practical decisions short of the balance required to navigate a long season properly.

title: Miami Heat legend Udonis Haslem ‘proud to announce’ ownership stake in Premier League soccer club

fullText:
Udonis Haslem is expanding his business portfolio with an investment in a newly promoted Premier League soccer club.

The popularity of soccer has skyrocketed in the US following the conclusion of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The sport has gained a plethora of new fans.

This apparently includes Miami Heat legend and former NBA star Udonis Haslem, who has decided to pour in some of his hard-earned money into a newly promoted English Premier League club.

After playing for two decades in the NBA, Haslem has transitioned into an analyst role, primarily for Amazon Prime Video's coverage.

Haslem is now further branching out as the Heat legend announced his investment in newly promoted PL club, Ipswich Town on X.

"Basketball has been my life, but I've always respected the culture and impact of football. Proud to announce that last September, I became a minority owner of Ipswich Town Football Club.

"When I first saw the club's motto 'Running Towards Adversity,' I knew this was a club I wanted to be part of. Something I've believed in my entire career," Haslem wrote on X.

He added, "Then I met the people behind the club, and it became clear it was more than just words. It's who they are. That's the only kind of culture I want to be around.

"I'm excited to support what's being built at Ipswich…both on and off the pitch. Miami to Portman Road. NBA to the Premier League. Let's go, Blues!"

Haslem spent his entire career following the ever-so-famous Heat culture, and it feels like the NBA legend has found a club that perfectly embodies that sentiment.

title: Three words to describe how I currently feel about Newcastle United
description: Newcastle United fans preparing for the 2026/27 Premier League season. Less than three weeks to go now until Liverpool travel to St James’ Park.
fullText:
Newcastle United fans preparing for the 2026/27 Premier League season.

Less than three weeks to go now until Liverpool travel to St James' Park.

An 'interesting' summer so far…

An ideal time to get a snapshot of views from Newcastle United fans on their thoughts.

So we sent out questions to a number of regular/irregular contributors to The Mag, varying to a degree the questions that different fans received to answer.

Next up answering some questions is Matt Busby said to Joe Harvey…:

Three words to describe how you currently feel as a Newcastle United fan?

Three words to describe Newcastle United now?

Do you see it as good news or bad news that Eddie Howe resigned?

Look, the man walks on water for what he has achieved but the conditions that led to what he achieved have changed. And for that reason, he didn't want to be here any longer. So in the circumstances, it's got to be a good thing he's departed, hasn't it?

Hand on heart, what position do you currently believe Newcastle United are most likely to finish in the 2026/27 Premier League season?

Without the distraction of Europe, we have got to be aiming for a European spot surely?

If Eddie Howe had stayed would your 2026/27 prediction have been different (up or down…)?

I think I've been persuaded that he wasn't up for re-inventing the side so I'd probably suggest we wouldn't finish any higher.

If Bruno leaves, who do you think would be best choice of NUFC captain?

I'd consider giving it to Lewis Hall, assuming he's not bound for pastures new as well. The guy seems as smart off the park as he does on it and I reckon there's a proper leader in there.

The opening six league games are Liverpool home, Spurs away, Bournemouth home, Leeds away, Hull home and Coventry away. How many points would Newcastle need to take for you to be happy and what would you predict will be the reality?

Despite two bogey teams visitingSt James' Park early doors , I think we can win all three home games. I'd also fancy us to pick up another four points from the away trips, so that's 13 from 18, and I'd be very content with that.

With so much change, how do you currently feel when it comes to balancing fears of the end of a relatively successful era and hopes of the dawning of the chance of a new successful different era? (So if you have 100% fears and 0% hopes that would be 100/0, if feeling 60% fear and 40% hope then 60/40)

I reckon 35:65 is my ratio. In other words, whilst I think there's a 1 in 3 chance that we'll blow up, I reckon there's a 2 in 3 chance of us kicking on. As above, if we can plunder 13 points from our first 6 games, any fears I have will be consigned to the dustbin.

Anthony Gordon leaving, your thoughts?

I think he lost faith when we were seemingly prepared to offload him when we hit the PSR buffers in June 2024, and it seems to me that he became selfish and as a result, his form more erratic and the consistency we'd previously seen/expected disappeared somewhat.

Hearing him speak in Spanish when signing for Barcelona seemed to reinforce the fact that he was hell bent on leaving us for Iberia.

When the lad was on fire, he was great, and it might be that the £70 million the Catalans have paid is seen as a steal, but he had a tendency to lose his head when the stakes were high and the history books will show he wasn't on the park when we lifted our first trophy in donkey's years (despite his endeavour in both legs of the semi final).

Long winded way of me saying, I'm not too concerned that AG has left Newcastle United.

Toure

What do you now see as the minimum Newcastle United need to achieve this coming season?

A European berth and a decent crack at one of the cups.

Predict the top six in the Premier League (in order) and which three clubs will be relegated in 2026/27.

1 Man City
2 Man Utd
3 Arsenal

5 Aston Villa
